title: Two Kellers, one clipboard
setting: Morning admission desk before a planned consultation.
hook: Mara arrives holding a letter addressed to M. Keller. So does the man beside her. The reception printer has produced two nearly identical labels and looks extremely pleased with itself. Mara starts explaining her cough while the trainee is already opening a record. She is eager to return to her bakery before the lunchtime queue, but the first useful question is not about coughing. It is about identity. A warm introduction and a careful check can prevent a very confident conversation with the wrong chart.
question: Both labels say M. Keller. What comes first?
options: Open the record with a cough note
Ask Mara to state her identifiers
Let the other Keller choose
feedback: The identity check comes before the symptom history is attached to a record. A cough note could belong to someone else, and another patient cannot validate Mara’s identity. A short explanation keeps the check friendly while making clear that a matching initial is not enough.
handover: Frau Mara Keller, 42 Jahre, berichtet über Husten. Vor der weiteren Anamnese wird wegen zweier ähnlich beschrifteter Unterlagen die Identität abgeglichen; eine Untersuchung ist noch nicht erfolgt.
focus: Confirm identity before attaching a history to a record.

title: The dictionary can wait outside
setting: First conversation in an outpatient examination room.
hook: Emil has brought reading glasses, a medication bag and the determination to understand what happens today. The trainee opens with “We will elicit your vegetative anamnesis.” Emil looks at the tiny pot plant on the desk and asks whether the fern is also being interviewed. His smile is an invitation to reset, not permission to continue with unexplained terminology. The consultation concerns several weeks of poor sleep. The challenge is to gather accurate information without making everyday experiences sound like a secret society’s entrance examination.
question: How should the trainee recover?
options: Explain the Latin root
Skip sleep to save time
Use ordinary questions and follow his answer
feedback: Ordinary questions keep the subject accessible and produce a clearer history. A lesson in Latin answers a question Emil did not ask. Skipping sleep would lose his main concern. His little joke is useful feedback about the wording, not evidence that his sleep problem is trivial.
handover: Herr Brandt, 58 Jahre, berichtet über nächtliches Erwachen gegen drei Uhr bei nach eigenen Angaben ungestörtem Einschlafen. Dauer und Auslöser der Durchschlafstörung sind noch zu erheben; weitere vegetative Angaben liegen nicht vor.
focus: Switch from professional terminology to ordinary patient language.

title: The phone has its own appointment
setting: A non-urgent history is interrupted by repeated work messages.
hook: Nora’s phone lights up every thirty seconds: the office cannot find the shared folder, then the key, then apparently the concept of lunch. She is here about recurrent headaches and keeps starting a sentence before another message arrives. The trainee becomes tempted to race through questions between vibrations. Nora apologises and says she needs five uninterrupted minutes herself. The task is to agree on a workable conversation, not scold her or diagnose the headaches from the fact that she has an irritating manager.
question: What should restart the conversation?
options: Agree on a pause, then return to the symptom story
Ask three questions while she texts
Record stress headache as confirmed
feedback: The agreed pause lets Nora participate and gives the history a reliable starting point. Multiple questions during texting invite partial answers. Calling this a confirmed stress headache jumps from context to diagnosis without assessment, even though the work messages are clearly an unwelcome part of her morning.
handover: Frau Feld, 36 Jahre, stellt sich wegen wiederkehrender Kopfschmerzen vor. Das Gespräch wurde durch Arbeitsnachrichten unterbrochen; eine vollständige Schmerzanamnese und Untersuchung stehen noch aus.
focus: Negotiate a brief agenda and manage interruptions respectfully.

title: The box that wanted a tick
setting: The trainee writes a history summary after an interrupted interview.
hook: Oskar has described leg discomfort and his regular blood-pressure medicine. Before the allergy question, a colleague calls the trainee away. On return, the documentation template is open, with a neat row of empty boxes that seem to disapprove of untidiness. “No known allergies” would make the page look finished. Oskar, meanwhile, is asking whether there is somewhere to charge his hearing aid. Nothing in the conversation has established his allergy history. A beautiful form can still tell a very ugly little lie.
question: Which entry is faithful to the interview?
options: No known allergies
Allergy history not yet obtained
Allergy unlikely
feedback: Only “not yet obtained” matches the available information. An empty field does not establish absence, and likelihood is not the question the record needs answered. The clinician should complete the history when possible, while preserving the distinction between an unanswered question and an explicitly negative answer.
handover: Herr Lind, 64 Jahre, berichtet über Beinbeschwerden und die Einnahme eines Blutdruckmedikaments. Die Allergieanamnese wurde wegen einer Unterbrechung noch nicht erhoben; der Medikamentenname ist ebenfalls noch zu klären.
focus: Document missing information without manufacturing normal findings.

title: The calendar disagreement
setting: A colleague asks for a concise presentation after a first history.
hook: Leonie says her cough has been “bad for three days.” Her first cough, however, began three weeks ago, during a move involving more cardboard than anyone remembers buying. The trainee’s note says simply “cough for three days.” At handover, that shorter version sounds tidy but changes the story. Leonie has not contradicted herself: she has described two different dates. The learner’s job is to separate onset from worsening, confirm the distinction, and carry both pieces into the professional presentation without turning the handover into a moving-house documentary.
question: What belongs in the opening handover sentence?
options: Only the worst day
The moving date
Three weeks of cough, worse for three days
feedback: The full timeline preserves both duration and deterioration. Giving only the worst day loses two weeks of symptoms, while the moving date is context rather than the symptom history itself. A short confirmation with Leonie turns a plausible interpretation into an accurately attributed patient report.
handover: Frau Hart, 29 Jahre, berichtet über seit drei Wochen bestehenden Husten mit deutlicher Zunahme seit drei Tagen. Eine Untersuchung und weitere Angaben zu Begleitsymptomen liegen noch nicht vor.
focus: Preserve onset and deterioration as separate time points.

title: The doorway is not a handover room
setting: A colleague requests a patient update beside a busy waiting area.
hook: Sami has just shared personal information during a consultation. Outside, a colleague asks, “What is his story?” Two other patients are sitting within easy hearing distance, and a delivery worker is wrestling a trolley through the doorway. The learner could provide a beautifully structured handover here, with flawless terminology and a very real audience problem. Sami can see both clinicians from his chair. Good communication includes choosing where to speak, not merely finding the perfect opening sentence while confidential details drift across the waiting room.
question: What should happen before the clinical summary?
options: Move to a suitable private place
Use only initials but stay there
Ask the waiting patients not to listen
feedback: Changing location addresses the actual problem: people who are not involved can hear the exchange. Initials cannot hide a recognisable story, and asking strangers not to listen is not a reliable boundary. The handover remains necessary; the setting is what needs to change first.
handover: Herr Winter, 47 Jahre, hat im Aufnahmegespräch persönliche Angaben gemacht. Die fachliche Übergabe erfolgt im geschützten Rahmen; klinische Einzelheiten sind in dieser Kommunikationsszene nicht angegeben.
focus: Choose an appropriate setting for professional communication.

title: The nod that meant maybe
setting: The end of a routine explanation before planned blood sampling.
hook: Tessa nods politely through an explanation of the next steps. She has nodded at three unfamiliar words and one sentence that seemed to have no landing place. When asked whether she understands, she says yes: she does not want to look difficult. Her real question is whether she should remain in this room or join the queue outside. The trainee has explained the science but not the next five minutes. A useful closing check should test the explanation, not put Tessa on the spot with a surprise oral examination.
question: Which check invites an honest answer?
options: You understood everything, yes?
Tell me the next step so I can check my explanation
Repeat every medical term
feedback: A concrete next-step question reveals whether the plan is usable. A yes-or-no question may invite polite agreement, and repeating terminology measures memory more than understanding. Tessa’s uncertainty is useful information that lets the trainee improve the explanation before she walks into the wrong queue.
handover: Frau Berg, 51 Jahre, wurde über eine geplante Blutentnahme informiert. Im Rückgespräch zeigte sich eine Unklarheit zum Warteort, die erläutert wurde; medizinische Befunde werden in dieser Szene nicht berichtet.
focus: Use teach-back as a check of the explanation.

title: The case nobody rehearsed
setting: A simulated examination conversation takes an unexpected turn.
hook: Hanna is a fictional patient in a practice session. The learner has memorised a beautiful opening for abdominal pain, including a transition polished to museum quality. Hanna instead begins, “I came because I am worried about a letter I received.” The learner’s eyes return to the rehearsed page. The exercise is not to prove that the script predicts the exam; it is to notice the person who is speaking now. The letter may matter, but its contents have not yet been established, and neither has Hanna’s main concern.
question: What is the best opening response to Hanna?
options: Return to the memorised symptom list
Promise the letter is harmless
Explore her concern and the actual letter
feedback: The learner should establish what Hanna received and why it worries her. Redirecting immediately would ignore her opening, while reassurance without reading or understanding the letter would invent certainty. The practice succeeds when its structure helps the conversation, even if the expected topic never arrives.
handover: Frau Reim, 33 Jahre, äußert Sorge wegen eines erhaltenen medizinischen Schreibens. Dessen Inhalt und die aktuelle Beschwerdesituation sind noch nicht geklärt; eine Diagnose lässt sich daraus nicht ableiten.
focus: Use a practice structure flexibly without treating it as a prediction.

title: The little blue tablet has no surname
setting: Medication history during a planned clinic visit.
hook: Jule is excellent at remembering birthdays and hopeless at remembering tablet names. She describes one as blue, one as round, and one as “the one my husband keeps moving.” Her phone contains a photograph of last year’s medication plan, but a prescription changed last month. The learner wants a complete list before the next patient arrives. Guessing from colour would be quick, and wrong with impressive confidence. The useful next step is to find a reliable current source while recording what Jule actually remembers.
question: What should be recorded now?
options: A guessed medicine name
No medicines
Reported tablet use; name unconfirmed
feedback: Unconfirmed use is the faithful entry while the current medication is checked. A guessed name can become a false prescribing assumption, and “no medicines” discards information Jule did provide. The aim is not a perfectly filled list at any cost; it is a list whose certainty is clear.
handover: Frau Sommer, 61 Jahre, berichtet über die morgendliche Einnahme einer blauen Tablette. Der Wirkstoff ist unklar; ein älterer Medikamentenplan liegt vor, wurde laut Patientin jedoch inzwischen geändert.
focus: Reconcile an uncertain medication name against a current source.

title: The allergy box needs a story
setting: An admission form lists an antibiotic allergy without details.
hook: Ben points to “penicillin allergy” on an old card. He remembers becoming unwell after a childhood prescription, but his sister remembers a rash and his father remembers “something with the stomach.” Family memory has become a committee, and the committee has not kept minutes. The trainee could repeat the label without questions or dismiss it because the account is vague. Neither move helps. The conversation needs the reaction, its timing, what treatment was needed, and an honest statement of what Ben cannot reliably recall.
question: Which follow-up is most useful?
options: Ask what happened and when
Delete the allergy because memory is poor
Record anaphylaxis to be safe
feedback: The reaction story provides useful detail without inventing a diagnosis. Deleting an uncertain label can conceal risk, while recording anaphylaxis creates a different unsupported claim. Ben’s uncertainty belongs in the note alongside the existing label and the plan to clarify available evidence.
handover: Herr Adler, 40 Jahre, berichtet über einen früheren Eintrag einer Penicillinallergie. Er erinnert möglicherweise ein Exanthem im Kindesalter; Zeitpunkt, weitere Symptome und damalige Behandlung sind noch unklar.
focus: Explore an allergy label without confirming or deleting it prematurely.

title: One glass, three different sizes
setting: A routine social history includes alcohol use.
hook: Ralf says he drinks “just a glass” in the evening. On his kitchen shelf, glasses range from a tiny celebration glass to something that could host a goldfish, so the phrase tells the learner less than it seems. He senses judgement and starts explaining how hard he works. The clinician’s task is to ask about the actual drink, amount and pattern without scoring Ralf’s character. A calm explanation of why the question matters can turn an awkward exchange into useful information for his care.
question: How do you clarify “one glass”?
options: Enter one unit automatically
Ask drink type, size and frequency
Ask whether he is a good driver
feedback: Type, size and frequency translate a vague phrase into usable information. Automatically assigning a unit pretends the missing quantity is known. A question about driving changes the subject and may feel accusatory. The immediate task is to understand Ralf’s pattern, not pass a verdict on him.
handover: Herr Meier, 55 Jahre, berichtet über abendlichen Weinkonsum. Glasgröße, genaue Menge und Häufigkeit sind noch zu konkretisieren; eine standardisierte Mengenangabe ist bislang nicht möglich.
focus: Ask about alcohol quantity without moral judgement.

title: The operation that did not count
setting: Past surgical history before a diagnostic consultation.
hook: Aylin says she has never had an operation. Later she mentions “the little camera in my knee” and a day spent at a surgical centre. In her mind an operation means a large incision and several nights in hospital; the knee procedure did not qualify. The trainee almost writes two contradictory entries. This is not a trap and Aylin has not tried to mislead anyone. She is using an everyday category, while the form uses a medical one. A short, respectful clarification can reconcile them.
question: What is the best next move?
options: Mark her history unreliable
Ignore the minor procedure
Clarify side, timing and what was done
feedback: Concrete questions resolve the apparent contradiction without blaming Aylin. Calling her unreliable confuses different word meanings with dishonesty. Ignoring the procedure loses relevant history. The exact operation remains unconfirmed, so the handover should report her description and the approximate timing rather than invent technical details.
handover: Frau Koch, 38 Jahre, berichtet nach Nachfrage über eine Arthroskopie des linken Knies vor etwa vier Jahren. Art des damaligen Eingriffs und Operationsbericht sind noch zu klären.
focus: Clarify everyday meanings of surgery and procedures.

title: Married does not mean someone is home
setting: Social history while considering whether a care plan is practical.
hook: Greta is married, lives with her husband and answers “yes” when asked whether she has family. The trainee nearly ticks “support available.” Then Greta explains that her husband needs help dressing and cannot manage the stairs. Their daughter lives two hours away and works nights. Greta has a remarkably organised wall calendar, but the calendar cannot lift shopping bags. The task is to ask who can actually help with specific needs, rather than treating a relationship status as a ready-made discharge arrangement.
question: Which fact is safe to hand over?
options: Daughter may help; availability unconfirmed
Full family support arranged
No family exists
feedback: The daughter is a possible source of support, not yet a confirmed arrangement. Reporting full support would erase the practical uncertainty. Saying no family exists is also false. The useful handover names both Greta’s caring role and the need to clarify who can help with concrete tasks.
handover: Frau Blum, 72 Jahre, lebt mit ihrem pflegebedürftigen Ehemann zusammen und versorgt ihn nach eigenen Angaben. Die Tochter kommt als Unterstützung infrage, ihre Verfügbarkeit ist jedoch nicht geklärt.
focus: Turn social labels into concrete support information.

title: A family history with a question mark
setting: A family-history question raises an uncertain cancer account.
hook: Jonas remembers that his father had “something in the bowel.” He was a teenager at the time, and adults discussed it in the kitchen after sending him upstairs. A cousin now calls it cancer; an aunt calls it inflammation. Jonas is worried that either version means the same thing will happen to him. The learner must not select the most dramatic label to make the record sound complete. This conversation needs both factual uncertainty and space for the fear that brought the family story into the room.
question: What should the note say?
options: Father definitely had cancer
Bowel operation reported; diagnosis uncertain
Family history negative
feedback: The operation is reported, while its reason remains uncertain. A definite cancer entry adds a fact nobody has established. A negative family history would discard the concern entirely. The next discussion can explore how to clarify the history without promising that Jonas is either destined for illness or free of risk.
handover: Herr Krug, 46 Jahre, berichtet über eine Darmoperation seines Vaters. Die zugrunde liegende Erkrankung und das Alter bei Diagnosestellung sind unklar; der Patient äußert Sorge bezüglich eines eigenen Erkrankungsrisikos.
focus: Attribute uncertain family diagnoses and respond to inherited-risk fears.

title: The tea that escaped the medication list
setting: A medication review includes products bought without prescription.
hook: Mina says she takes only her prescribed thyroid medicine. As she searches her bag, a packet of herbal sleep capsules appears beside a vitamin bottle and a folded shopping receipt long enough to qualify as literature. She does not count these as medicines because they come from a shop rather than a doctor. The learner should not laugh at that distinction or declare every supplement dangerous. The job is to invite a complete list, clarify what she uses, and leave interaction assessment to a proper review.
question: What is the useful response to the capsules?
options: Ignore all shop-bought products
Tell her to stop everything
Add and identify them for review
feedback: The products belong in the history even when they were not prescribed. Ignoring them leaves the list incomplete, while an instruction to stop everything would skip the assessment the conversation is meant to support. Thanking Mina for the clarification makes future disclosure easier and keeps the review collaborative.
handover: Frau Weber, 49 Jahre, berichtet über eine Schilddrüsenmedikation sowie pflanzliche Schlafkapseln und Vitamine. Präparate, Inhaltsstoffe und Einnahmehäufigkeit werden anhand der Packungen noch abgeglichen.
focus: Include non-prescription and herbal products without blaming the patient.

title: Five kilos needs a calendar
setting: A vegetative history includes reported weight change.
hook: Theo says he has lost five kilos and waits for the clinician’s reaction. That could describe an intended change over a year or a recent change he cannot explain. His trousers have noticed, but trousers are poor historians. The trainee needs the starting weight, approximate dates and whether Theo was trying to lose weight. He has not brought measurements, only a memory of using a friend’s scale. The conversation should make the uncertainty visible without turning an approximate report into a precise trend chart.
question: Which detail most changes the meaning of Theo’s opening?
options: Time period and whether it was intended
Trouser brand
Whether he owns a scale
feedback: Time and intention turn the opening number into a meaningful history. The trouser brand does not help, and owning a scale alone does not establish a reliable trend. The reported loss remains approximate, but its unplanned nature and possible timescale can now be passed on honestly for assessment.
handover: Herr Frank, 57 Jahre, berichtet über einen geschätzten unbeabsichtigten Gewichtsverlust von etwa fünf Kilogramm in möglicherweise zwei Monaten. Vergleichbare Messwerte sowie weitere vegetative Angaben liegen noch nicht vor.
focus: Clarify amount, timescale and intention in weight change.

title: The questionnaire can wait for a person
setting: A history-taking session is interrupted by significant pain.
hook: Malika tries to answer politely but keeps losing her place because the pain is difficult to tolerate. The learner has reached only the second page of the form and worries about finishing. Malika asks whether pain relief is something she must earn by completing the questions. The task is to respond to the person in front of the paperwork: assess urgency, involve the responsible team promptly and consider pain care without promising a particular medicine before relevant checks. A complete interview is not a prize for enduring discomfort quietly.
question: What should happen before the remaining routine questions?
options: A promise to endure
Assessment and appropriate help for the pain
A lecture about time limits
feedback: Assessment and appropriate help respond to Malika’s current need and may improve her ability to give a history. A promise to endure or a time-limit lecture treats pain as an inconvenience to the form. The learner should act without inventing a treatment order or guaranteeing complete relief.
handover: Frau Stein, 45 Jahre, berichtet über Schmerzen, die ihre Konzentration im Anamnesegespräch deutlich beeinträchtigen. Das Routinegespräch wird pausiert und eine zeitnahe klinische Beurteilung einschließlich Schmerzmanagement veranlasst; Ursache und weitere Befunde sind noch offen.
focus: Respond to pain without making relief conditional on finishing the interview.

title: The question beneath the question
setting: A patient asks whether unexplained symptoms mean cancer.
hook: Henriette asks, “Could it be cancer?” Her mother died after a late diagnosis, and every unanswered test now feels like the beginning of the same story. The learner is tempted to say “Do not think like that” to restore calm. That would leave the fear untouched and the uncertainty hidden. The task is to ask what brought the concern forward, acknowledge its personal meaning and explain what is known and still being assessed. Henriette needs an honest conversation, not a guarantee or an invitation to imagine the worst.
question: Which response addresses both meaning and facts?
options: Dismiss the cancer word
Confirm cancer from the family story
Acknowledge the fear and explain the actual assessment
feedback: Acknowledging the fear and explaining the assessment answers both parts of Henriette’s concern. Dismissal may repeat the experience she fears, while confirmation from family history invents a diagnosis. The learner should show that the symptoms are being considered without pretending the results are already known.
handover: Frau Falk, 57 Jahre, äußert Sorge vor einer malignen Erkrankung vor dem Hintergrund einer späten Krebsdiagnose ihrer Mutter. Die aktuelle Diagnose ist offen; Sorgen und weitere Abklärung werden besprochen, ohne eine Entwarnung oder Bestätigung vorwegzunehmen.
focus: Explore a feared diagnosis without dismissing or confirming it.

title: A useful I do not know
setting: A patient asks a technical question the learner cannot reliably answer.
hook: Benedikt asks whether a proposed examination could interact with a device mentioned in an old report. The learner recognises half the terminology and could assemble a sentence that sounds impressively medical. The other half would be guesswork wearing a white coat. Benedikt does not need a fluent invention; he needs the question checked before the relevant decision. The task is to acknowledge the limit, identify who can answer and give a concrete follow-up route, rather than postponing the question indefinitely or pretending that confidence makes an answer true.
question: What makes the admission of uncertainty useful?
options: A named clarification step before the decision
A vague promise to answer someday
A confident guess to keep trust
feedback: A concrete clarification step gives Benedikt a reliable process despite the knowledge gap. A vague promise leaves the issue floating, and a confident guess creates false reassurance. The learner should ensure the specific information is reviewed by the appropriate professional before the relevant examination decision.
handover: Herr Reim, 53 Jahre, fragt nach der Verträglichkeit einer geplanten Untersuchung mit einem medizinischen Gerät. Gerätetyp und Kompatibilität sind noch nicht verifiziert; vor der Entscheidung wird fachliche Rücksprache veranlasst.
focus: State a knowledge limit and take ownership of getting clarification.

title: The face is young; the answer can be grown-up
setting: A patient questions a learner’s experience and asks for a senior clinician.
hook: Rita studies the learner and says, “You look younger than my grandson. Can I speak to someone experienced?” The learner feels stung and considers listing every qualification earned since school. Rita’s concern may come from a previous difficult experience, but nobody has asked. The task is to explain the learner’s role honestly, acknowledge the request and arrange appropriate senior involvement without defensiveness or invented years of experience. A calm response can keep the conversation useful; it does not require winning an argument about anyone’s face.
question: What is the strongest response?
options: Invent additional experience
Clarify the role and arrange appropriate senior input
Refuse because the request is rude
feedback: Honest role clarity and appropriate senior input address the actual request. Inventing experience undermines trust, and refusing on the basis of hurt feelings makes the consultation about the learner. Asking about the earlier experience can also reveal what Rita needs explained before she feels able to participate.
handover: Frau Sommer, 79 Jahre, wünscht aufgrund einer früheren übersehenen Erkrankung ein Gespräch mit einer erfahrenen ärztlichen Person. Eigene Rolle und Zuständigkeit werden erläutert und die verantwortliche Kollegin wird hinzugezogen.
focus: Respond to doubts about experience with honest role clarity and appropriate escalation.

title: The second question needs a reason
setting: A clinician repeats an important detail after not hearing it clearly.
hook: Milan has already said his medication name twice. A noisy corridor swallowed the ending both times, but he thinks the learner has simply not listened. When the question comes again, he folds his arms. The learner could blame his speed or write the closest familiar name to end the tension. Neither solves the problem. The task is to explain the specific listening gap, ask for the information in a different form and read it back. The conversation needs a small repair, not a contest about who is speaking correctly.
question: What should change after two failed attempts?
options: Guess the closest name
Ask the same way without explanation
Explain the gap and use packaging or spelling
feedback: Explaining the gap and changing the channel makes the repeat purposeful. Guessing risks a false medication entry, while another unexplained repetition can deepen the feeling of not being heard. Reading back the final detail gives Milan a chance to confirm the repair rather than merely endure it.
handover: Bei Herrn Fox, 48 Jahre, wurde ein Medikamentenname wegen Umgebungsgeräuschen zunächst nicht sicher verstanden. Die Identifikation erfolgt anhand der Packung mit Rückbestätigung; bis dahin bleibt der Name ungesichert.
focus: Repair repeated clarification requests without blaming the speaker.

title: The story has a side street
setting: A non-urgent consultation drifts away from the main symptom.
hook: Pauline begins describing dizziness, then tells a long story about her neighbour’s renovation, the broken doorbell and a parcel delivered to the wrong building. The learner can see the remaining time shrinking and wants to say, “That is irrelevant.” Yet the story may contain stress, sleep disruption or a practical problem that matters. The task is to acknowledge what was heard, identify the immediate clinical priority and ask permission to return to it. A respectful redirect should make the conversation clearer without making Pauline feel that she herself is the interruption.
question: Which redirect is most effective?
options: Acknowledge briefly, then ask a focused symptom question
Call the whole story irrelevant
Let all priorities disappear
feedback: A brief acknowledgement followed by a specific question preserves rapport and direction. Dismissing the whole story may hide relevant context and discourage participation. Allowing every priority to disappear also fails the consultation. The learner should guide the conversation without treating the patient as a problem to manage.
handover: Frau Heller, 56 Jahre, berichtet über Schwindel und zusätzliche Alltagsbelastungen. Das Gespräch wird wertschätzend zur zeitlichen Symptomabfolge zurückgeführt; Beginn, Begleitsymptome und Untersuchung sind noch zu klären.
focus: Redirect a long narrative with acknowledgement and a shared agenda.

title: A private question with a clear reason
setting: Before a proposed investigation, a clinician needs relevant pregnancy information.
hook: Lea is discussing a possible imaging examination with her partner sitting beside her. The learner needs to ask whether pregnancy is possible but is unsure how to introduce the subject. A blunt assumption based on age, relationship status or appearance would be unhelpful. Lea also may not want to discuss personal details in front of her partner. The task is to explain why the question matters, offer a private conversation and leave the imaging decision to an individual benefit-risk assessment rather than repeating a blanket rule that all imaging is forbidden.
question: What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Ask the partner to answer
Explain the reason, offer privacy and seek individual review
Assume pregnancy is impossible from appearance
feedback: The reason and privacy offer support an accurate, voluntary answer. A partner cannot automatically answer for Lea, and appearance cannot establish pregnancy status. The information should guide an individual examination discussion rather than a blanket claim that every imaging option is prohibited or safe.
handover: Frau Winter, 27 Jahre, wünscht zur Frage einer möglichen Schwangerschaft ein Gespräch ohne ihren Partner. Der Status ist noch ungeklärt; die geplante Bildgebung wird nach Erhebung der relevanten Angaben individuell mit dem zuständigen Team besprochen.
focus: Ask a sensitive pregnancy question privately and avoid blanket imaging claims.

title: The scan does not come with a kitchen knife
setting: A routine imaging explanation reveals a literal misunderstanding of technical language.
hook: Wolfram hears that an examination creates “slice images” and looks alarmed. He asks whether anyone will actually cut him. The learner almost laughs, then realises the phrase has never been explained. Wolfram understands the world through concrete images; the problem is the wording, not his intelligence. A gentle clarification can make the idea memorable without making him the joke. The task is to explain that the term describes how images are displayed, check what else sounds unclear and avoid expanding the analogy into claims about a specific scan’s safety or suitability.
question: What should the learner repair?
options: Wolfram’s intelligence
The patient’s sense of humour
The unexplained meaning of the imaging term
feedback: The missing explanation is the problem. Neither intelligence nor humour needs correction. Clarifying the term and the actual procedure makes the conversation usable, while a respectful response encourages further questions. The learner should not let a helpful analogy become a promise about every aspect of an unspecified examination.
handover: Herr Maier, 52 Jahre, verstand den Begriff Schnittbild zunächst als körperlichen Schnitt. Die bildbezogene Bedeutung wurde erläutert; Details der konkret geplanten Untersuchung werden gesondert besprochen.
focus: Repair a literal misunderstanding with a respectful visual explanation.

title: The bench between home and bread
setting: A clinic visit for recurring calf pain during walking.
hook: Alfons used to walk to the bakery without thinking about the route. Now he stops at the bench outside the florist, studies the window, and tells his wife he has developed an interest in bouquets. In truth, his right calf hurts and improves after a pause. The learner needs a practical walking distance and a clear symptom pattern, not a guess based on how fit Alfons looks. His hidden worry is that losing this small daily routine will mean depending on others for everything.
question: Which question develops the walking story?
options: Why do you like flowers?
What happens after you stop?
Can you prove the distance?
feedback: The response to stopping clarifies the symptom pattern without shaming Alfons or demanding unrealistic precision. The florist is a useful landmark, not the clinical subject. His distance can remain approximate while the clinician explores the symptoms and arranges an assessment of possible causes.
handover: Herr Berger, 59 Jahre, berichtet über Schmerzen der rechten Wade nach etwa 200 Metern Gehen, die sich nach einer Pause besserten. Weitere Beschwerden und Gefäßbefunde sind noch zu erheben; eine pAVK ist eine mögliche Erklärung.
focus: Convert a familiar route into a careful exertional symptom history.

title: When the sofa no longer helps
setting: Follow-up for leg pain whose pattern has changed.
hook: Helga was previously asked about discomfort during walking. Today she says her foot also hurts when she rests at night. She brought the same shopping bag as last time, so a hurried learner might treat this as the same visit with a new date. Helga is not asking for a more elegant definition of circulation; she wants to know why the old pattern has changed. The task is to notice the new rest symptom, communicate its importance and seek prompt clinical assessment rather than replay the previous advice.
question: What matters most in today’s opening?
options: Her bag is familiar
The earlier walking distance is exact
The pain now occurs at rest
feedback: The new rest symptom changes the conversation and requires reassessment. Familiar surroundings and old details should not hide it. The story does not establish the cause or severity on its own, so the learner should communicate concern and seek appropriate evaluation rather than announce a stage or repeat old advice.
handover: Frau Dorn, 67 Jahre, berichtet seit zwei Nächten über neu aufgetretene Fußschmerzen in Ruhe, zuvor nur beim Gehen. Eine zeitnahe klinische Beurteilung ist erforderlich; Seitenangabe, Gefäßstatus und weitere Warnzeichen sind noch zu klären.
focus: Recognise a changed symptom pattern and communicate the need for reassessment.

title: A cold foot changes the whole appointment
setting: An assessment is interrupted by a report of sudden foot changes.
hook: Farid was waiting to discuss weeks of leg discomfort. During the conversation he reports that his left foot suddenly became very painful and cold about twenty minutes ago. He now finds it hard to move his toes and asks whether he should finish the form first. The learner has not examined him and must not invent a pulse finding. The priority has changed: an urgent circulation problem is possible. The useful words are short, direct and connected to action, while the routine history and paperwork wait.
question: What is the next communication move?
options: Stop and call the clinical team
Complete the form together
Reassure him that cold feet are common
feedback: Immediate escalation matches the sudden change with possible serious circulation compromise. Completing the form delays assessment, and generic reassurance ignores the combination of pain, coldness and movement difficulty. The handover should report these symptoms accurately while making clear that examination findings have not yet been established.
handover: Herr Stein, 62 Jahre, berichtet über seit etwa 20 Minuten plötzlich schmerzhaften, kalten linken Fuß mit eingeschränkter Zehenbewegung. Bei Verdacht auf eine akute Durchblutungsstörung wird das Gespräch unterbrochen und sofort das ärztliche Team angefordert; Untersuchungsbefunde fehlen noch.
focus: Interrupt a routine interview for possible acute limb compromise.

title: Two roads, opposite directions
setting: A patient asks what suspected arterial disease means.
hook: Petra heard “vascular problem” and assumes it means the same thing as her sister’s venous clot. Her sister wore a compression stocking, so Petra has borrowed one and brought it in a tote bag labelled “just in case.” The learner needs to explain that arteries and veins have different jobs without delivering a full anatomy lecture. The practical issue is not winning a vocabulary quiz. It is preventing Petra from treating someone else’s diagnosis and equipment as an automatically suitable plan for her own leg symptoms.
question: What should Petra understand before any treatment choice?
options: A stocking confirms the diagnosis
Her own circulation needs assessment
Her sister’s outcome predicts hers
feedback: The useful message is that Petra needs an individual assessment. A stocking is equipment, not diagnostic evidence, and a relative’s experience cannot predict her own situation. The learner can explain the vessel distinction clearly while avoiding a premature recommendation about what she should apply to the leg.
handover: Frau Wald, 56 Jahre, fragt bei vermuteter arterieller Problematik nach der Übernahme einer Kompressionsversorgung ihrer Schwester. Eigene Gefäßbefunde liegen in dieser Szene nicht vor; die Indikation ist individuell zu prüfen.
focus: Distinguish arteries from veins in plain language without prescribing by analogy.

title: The lecture he has already heard
setting: A vascular assessment includes smoking history and support preferences.
hook: Uwe sees the smoking question and braces himself. He has reduced his cigarettes but has not stopped, and he expects the next ten minutes to become a lecture he can recite from memory. He also has a real question about leg pain and worries that admitting continued smoking will make the clinician less interested in helping him. The learner needs the history and can offer support, but blame will not make the numbers more accurate. The conversation should leave room for Uwe’s effort, barriers and priorities.
question: What response keeps both history and support possible?
options: Demand a promise to stop today
Skip the subject forever
Explore the pattern and offer support
feedback: Exploring the pattern gives a usable history and opens a voluntary discussion of support. A demanded promise may produce agreement without a realistic plan. Avoiding the subject forever loses relevant information. The learner can be clear about clinical relevance while avoiding blame and keeping attention on Uwe’s symptoms.
handover: Herr Seidel, 63 Jahre, berichtet über fortgesetzten, gegenüber früher reduzierten Nikotinkonsum mit stressabhängiger Zunahme. Genaue Mengen und Dauer sind noch zu erheben; Unterstützungsangebote werden mit seinem Einverständnis besprochen.
focus: Discuss smoking neutrally and ask permission before offering support.

title: The appointment has another patient at home
setting: A patient with leg symptoms is worried about her dependent partner.
hook: Rosa keeps checking the clock. Her partner needs help with lunch, and she has not told him this appointment might take longer than a quick prescription. When further assessment is mentioned, she reaches for her coat. The learner could interpret this as refusing care, but Rosa is trying to meet two responsibilities at once. Her daily timetable is more tightly organised than the clinic’s, and that is saying something. The task is to uncover the practical concern while explaining why her own symptoms still need attention.
question: What should be clarified first about home?
options: The actual care need and possible contacts
Whether Rosa is being difficult
A guaranteed social-service arrival time
feedback: The actual care need is the starting point for a workable plan. Calling Rosa difficult ignores the competing responsibility. Promising an arrival time without an arrangement creates false reassurance. The clinician should address the barrier alongside the medical explanation, keeping urgency and unconfirmed support visible.
handover: Frau Ahrens, 65 Jahre, äußert bei weiterer Abklärung ihrer Beinbeschwerden Sorge um die Versorgung ihres Partners. Eine Nachbarin kommt möglicherweise infrage; Unterstützung ist noch nicht bestätigt, und die medizinische Dringlichkeit wird erläutert.
focus: Explore a caregiving barrier without promising an unarranged solution.

title: Will the ultrasound open the pipe?
setting: Explaining a proposed vascular ultrasound investigation.
hook: David hears “scan of the blood vessels” and imagines a tiny device travelling through his leg, clearing a path as it goes. He asks whether he should arrange a lift home because the “repair” might take hours. The learner has described the test name but not its purpose. David is an electrician and understands equipment beautifully when someone explains what it actually does. The challenge is to distinguish looking from treating, explain the proposed examination in ordinary terms and invite questions without promising a particular result.
question: Which distinction does David need?
options: A scan guarantees a cure
The test assesses; treatment is a separate discussion
Every vessel scan requires surgery
feedback: David needs to understand the purpose of the proposed test. A cure promise confuses assessment with treatment, while saying surgery is always needed invents a pathway. A clear distinction lets him ask useful practical questions and participate in the next decision once information is available.
handover: Herr Falk, 54 Jahre, wurde über eine geplante Gefäßultraschalluntersuchung zur diagnostischen Abklärung informiert. Er hatte zunächst eine Behandlung erwartet; ein Untersuchungsergebnis oder eine Therapieentscheidung liegt noch nicht vor.
focus: Separate a diagnostic investigation from an intervention.

title: Seven out of ten, but when?
setting: A trainee prepares a summary of activity-related leg discomfort.
hook: Karin gives her pain a seven. The trainee writes the number in a large box and feels productive. Then Karin adds that it is much lower when she sits, worse on a hill and sometimes different after a long day. The number is useful, but it has acquired more authority than the story around it. Karin’s aim is to walk to her granddaughter’s school again, not achieve a more impressive score. The learner must tie severity to circumstances and function before handing the case over.
question: Which summary preserves Karin’s meaning?
options: Pain is always seven
School walk will be restored
Seven uphill, two sitting; walking goal noted
feedback: The contextual summary preserves the two reported scores and Karin’s goal. A constant seven erases the change with activity, while promising the school walk invents an outcome. Good communication makes the limitation clear enough for assessment without pretending a number or a wish settles the diagnosis or prognosis.
handover: Frau Vogt, 60 Jahre, gibt Beinschmerzen mit 7/10 beim Bergaufgehen und aktuell 2/10 im Sitzen an. Sie möchte die Strecke zur Schule ihrer Enkelin wieder bewältigen; genaue Gehstrecke und Befunde sind noch zu erheben.
focus: Attach pain severity to context and patient goals.

title: The holiday ended; the calf complaint did not
setting: Urgent assessment after a long road journey and new calf symptoms.
hook: Jonas returned from a caravan holiday with photographs, three bags of laundry and a painful swollen left calf. He blames the cramped seat and asks for something to rub on it before work. The drive lasted much of the day, but nobody has yet established when the swelling began or whether he has other symptoms. The learner should take the travel story seriously without declaring it proof of a clot. An urgent assessment is needed, and the first conversation must separate the symptom timeline from Jonas’s perfectly understandable explanation.
question: What is the best framing?
options: A clot is possible and needs urgent assessment
It is only a cramped muscle
Travel proves a clot
feedback: The possible clot deserves urgent assessment, while its presence remains unconfirmed. Calling it only a muscle problem dismisses the report; calling it proven confuses a risk context with diagnostic evidence. The symptom check also helps identify whether immediate emergency escalation is required instead of a routine history.
handover: Herr Hecht, 44 Jahre, berichtet seit gestern Abend nach längerer Autofahrt über eine schmerzhafte Schwellung der linken Wade. Eine TVT ist abzuklären; Angaben zu Atemnot und Thoraxschmerzen sowie Untersuchungsbefunde stehen noch aus.
focus: Explore a risk context without treating it as diagnostic proof.

title: Two complaints, one appointment
setting: A patient describes a blocked nose and new leg swelling together.
hook: Marek begins with the blocked nose that ruined his holiday sleep. He has assembled an impressive theory involving the caravan’s air conditioning, mountain weather and one suspicious pillow. Only near the end does he mention a newly swollen, painful calf. The learner must not reward the longest story with all the attention. Both concerns deserve to be heard, but their priority may differ. A respectful signpost can move the leg symptoms forward without telling Marek that the miserable nights he wanted to discuss do not matter.
question: How should the learner reorder the discussion?
options: Finish every nasal question first
Explain the calf priority and retain the nasal concern
Ignore both until a complete form exists
feedback: The learner should make the change of priority explicit and keep the other concern visible. Completing a long nasal history first could delay assessment of the new calf symptoms. Waiting for a complete form mistakes paperwork for care; the agenda should respond to the information that has just emerged.
handover: Herr Fink, 37 Jahre, berichtet über nasale Obstruktion und seit gestern neu geschwollene Wade mit Schmerzen. Die Wadensymptomatik wird priorisiert dringend abgeklärt; Seite, Begleitsymptome und Befunde sind noch zu erheben.
focus: Prioritise potentially urgent symptoms within a multi-complaint history.

title: The question that changes the room
setting: A possible DVT assessment is interrupted by sudden breathlessness.
hook: Eva came for a swollen leg. While describing the journey home, she suddenly says she cannot catch her breath and has chest pain. The learner was about to ask about an operation ten years ago. That question can wait. Eva looks frightened and asks whether this means the suspected clot has moved. No scan or examination result has established the cause. The communication task is to act urgently, state the concern without announcing a confirmed pulmonary embolism, and summon the clinical team rather than finish the interview.
question: What should happen now?
options: Complete past surgery questions
Wait until the leg scan is reported
Stop and summon the clinical team
feedback: Immediate escalation is the appropriate response to new breathlessness and chest pain. Finishing the history or waiting for a leg investigation delays assessment of the change. The learner should communicate a possible serious cause and the reported symptoms, not reassure falsely or pronounce a diagnosis without evidence.
handover: Frau Lorenz, 52 Jahre, entwickelt im Gespräch bei berichteter Beinschwellung neu Atemnot und Thoraxschmerzen. Eine Lungenembolie ist eine mögliche Ursache; das Gespräch wird unterbrochen und sofort klinische Unterstützung angefordert, Befunde liegen noch nicht vor.
focus: Escalate new breathlessness and chest pain without diagnostic overclaiming.

title: No breathlessness is not an all-clear stamp
setting: A patient answers a screening question during a leg assessment.
hook: Paul says he is not short of breath and smiles with relief: “Then it cannot be a clot, can it?” He would like to return to his shop before the delivery arrives. The trainee recognises the temptation to accept this tidy conclusion. A negative answer is useful, but it does not erase the painful swollen calf that brought Paul in. The task is to explain what has and has not been learned, preserve the reported negative accurately and continue the appropriate assessment without turning reassurance into a false guarantee.
question: Which statement is accurate?
options: Breathlessness denied; calf cause still unclarified
All serious causes excluded
No further assessment is needed
feedback: The accurate statement preserves the useful negative without exaggerating it. Neither all serious causes nor the need for assessment can be resolved by one symptom answer. Paul should understand that the calf complaint still deserves attention and that new symptoms should be reported immediately.
handover: Herr Beck, 50 Jahre, berichtet über eine schmerzhafte Wadenschwellung und verneint aktuell Atemnot. Eine TVT oder andere Ursache ist dadurch nicht ausgeschlossen; weitere Anamnese und Untersuchung sind erforderlich.
focus: Explain the limits of a negative symptom answer.

title: A scan is a question, not a verdict in advance
setting: Explaining an ultrasound proposed for suspected venous thrombosis.
hook: Nele hears the word “compression” and pictures someone squeezing her painful leg as a test of bravery. She asks whether the scan has already proved there is a clot. The appointment letter contains several technical terms and exactly zero helpful sketches. The learner needs to explain the purpose of the proposed ultrasound, invite her to mention discomfort, and avoid promising that it will be completely painless or settle every possible cause in one step. Nele wants a realistic picture of what is being proposed before agreeing.
question: What should the explanation include?
options: A guarantee of no discomfort
Purpose, process and invitation to speak up
A confirmed clot diagnosis
feedback: Purpose, process and a chance to ask questions create a realistic explanation. A guarantee of no discomfort is not justified, and a diagnosis before results confuses the reason for the test with its outcome. The learner should keep the proposed examination distinct from the conclusion that may follow.
handover: Frau Graf, 32 Jahre, wird über eine geplante Kompressionssonographie bei Thromboseverdacht informiert. Sie äußert Sorge vor Druckschmerz; ein Untersuchungsergebnis und eine gesicherte Diagnose liegen noch nicht vor.
focus: Explain diagnostic purpose and invite procedural questions.

title: The stocking stayed in the drawer
setting: A follow-up conversation explores difficulty with a prescribed compression plan.
hook: Ingo says he used the prescribed stocking “most days.” After a pause he admits it has stayed in the drawer this week because his hands hurt and he cannot pull it on alone. He expected a reprimand, so he first offered the version that sounded like a good patient. The instruction sheet has excellent diagrams but, inconveniently, no spare pair of hands. The learner needs to uncover the practical barrier and arrange appropriate review, not independently change compression or treat difficulty with equipment as a character flaw.
question: What question is most useful?
options: Why are you refusing care?
Will you promise never to miss it again?
What prevents you from putting it on?
feedback: Asking about the obstacle identifies the real problem: painful hands and unavailable help. A refusal label misdescribes it, and a promise does not create the missing ability or support. The learner should make the barrier visible so the responsible team can review a workable plan.
handover: Herr Maas, 58 Jahre, berichtet, den verordneten Kompressionsstrumpf diese Woche wegen schmerzhafter Hände nicht angelegt zu haben. Morgendliche Hilfe sei nicht verfügbar; Art der Verordnung und geeignete Unterstützung werden mit dem zuständigen Team geklärt.
focus: Explore a practical adherence barrier without blame.

title: Two boxes, one uncertain plan
setting: A medication reconciliation follows a recent care transition.
hook: Sven brings two medication boxes from different appointments. He calls both “blood thinners” and is unsure whether the newer one replaces the older one. His kitchen noticeboard now holds two plans and a supermarket coupon, all with similar coloured magnets. The learner should not choose a regimen from memory or tell him to take both to be safe. This is a communication and reconciliation problem requiring prompt clarification with the prescribing team, while the note records exactly what Sven says he has actually taken.
question: What comes before a new instruction?
options: Prompt reconciliation with the responsible team
Choose the newer-looking box
Assume both are the same drug
feedback: The conflict needs prompt reconciliation with reliable prescribing information. Box appearance and a shared nickname cannot identify the intended regimen. The learner should not improvise a dosing or stop-start instruction; the useful contribution is an accurate account of the competing plans and what Sven has actually taken.
handover: Herr Rohde, 69 Jahre, berichtet über zwei widersprüchliche Pläne für als Blutverdünner bezeichnete Medikamente. Präparate und tatsächliche letzte Einnahme werden erhoben; eine zeitnahe Klärung mit dem verordnenden Team ist erforderlich.
focus: Clarify possible duplicate anticoagulant instructions without giving an improvised regimen.

title: The left leg survived the story; not the summary
setting: A learner checks a draft handover before passing on suspected DVT.
hook: Rina has repeatedly described left calf pain. The trainee’s draft says right, inherited from a copied heading. Everything else looks polished: correct terminology, sensible order, impeccable punctuation. The wrong side is sitting in the middle wearing a very professional suit. Rina notices the word as the learner reads the summary aloud. The task is to welcome the correction, verify the side and update the record and spoken handover consistently. Defending the original note would protect the writer’s pride at the expense of useful information.
question: What is the complete repair?
options: Correct only the spoken version
Verify and correct all relevant versions
Ask Rina to ignore the typo
feedback: Verification followed by consistent correction repairs the communication chain. Fixing only the spoken version leaves a misleading record, and asking Rina to ignore it discourages a helpful safety check. The learner can acknowledge the error briefly without making the consultation about their own embarrassment.
handover: Frau Vogt, 41 Jahre, berichtet über Schmerzen und Schwellung der linken Wade. Eine zunächst fehlerhafte Rechtsangabe wurde nach Rückfrage korrigiert; objektive Befunde und Diagnose stehen noch aus.
focus: Correct a laterality error openly and consistently.

title: The sock was doing public relations
setting: A first wound consultation begins with reluctance to uncover the leg.
hook: Sina has chosen a long skirt and thick socks to hide the wet patch near her ankle. She apologises for the smell before anyone has asked a question. For months she has managed dressings around work and caring for her partner, hoping the wound would improve quietly. The learner’s first task is not to express surprise at how long she waited. It is to make the room feel safe enough for an honest account. The sock has been doing public relations; the wound now needs careful assessment.
question: What should open the assessment?
options: Criticise the delay
Offer privacy and ask permission
Assume the cause from the smell
feedback: Privacy and permission address Sina’s immediate barrier to examination. Criticism may make her minimise the history, while smell alone cannot establish the cause. The learner should gather details and seek clinical assessment without turning the consultation into a judgement about why she did not arrive earlier.
handover: Frau Wagner, 66 Jahre, berichtet über eine länger bestehende nässende Wunde im Knöchelbereich und äußert Scham. Dauer, Seitenangabe, aktuelle Veränderungen und Wundbefund werden noch erhoben.
focus: Reduce shame and invite an accurate wound history.

title: The dressing change needs a pause button
setting: A patient anticipates pain during a planned dressing change.
hook: Marlene becomes quiet when the dressing trolley arrives. Last time the change hurt, but she did not say anything because everyone looked busy. Today she asks whether she can “be brave enough” to finish it. The learner should not turn this into a test of toughness or promise that it will not hurt. A useful conversation establishes what happened before, how she can signal discomfort and which clinical support is needed. The trolley is well stocked with supplies; it also needs a plan the patient understands.
question: What should be agreed before starting?
options: A promise that it cannot hurt
That she will remain silent
How to report pain and pause
feedback: A clear way to report pain supports ongoing participation. An absolute comfort promise cannot be guaranteed, and asking for silence hides useful feedback. The team should consider her earlier experience and appropriate pain management rather than treating speed as the only measure of a successful dressing change.
handover: Frau Fox, 70 Jahre, berichtet über starke Schmerzen beim Ablösen des früheren Verbands. Vor dem geplanten Wechsel werden Vorgehen, Rückmeldemöglichkeit und Schmerzmanagement mit dem zuständigen Team abgestimmt; aktuelle Wundbefunde fehlen noch.
focus: Prepare for discomfort with consent and a clear pause signal.

title: The miracle cream has a missing label
setting: A wound history reveals irritation after a shop-bought cream.
hook: Bernd bought a cream after a neighbour called it “marvellous.” The tube now has a folded end, a rubbed-off label and a popularity rating of one enthusiastic neighbour. His skin became itchy and red after using it, but he is unsure whether the wound itself was already worsening. The learner must separate timing from assumed cause and identify the product if possible. This is not the moment to blame Bernd for trying to help himself or confidently label every new red patch as an allergy.
question: Which note is most accurate?
options: Itching and redness after an unidentified cream
All wound creams cause allergy
No reaction because the label is missing
feedback: The accurate note keeps the reported symptoms and timing without inventing the product or mechanism. A blanket allergy label is unsupported, while ignoring the event because the label is unreadable loses useful information. Identifying the cream and assessing the skin are the next clarification tasks.
handover: Herr Hase, 64 Jahre, berichtet über Juckreiz und Rötung am Abend nach Anwendung einer nicht identifizierten Wundsalbe. Eine Kontaktreaktion ist möglich, aber nicht gesichert; Produkt und Wundverlauf werden weiter geklärt.
focus: Clarify a possible topical reaction while preserving uncertainty.

title: The wound photograph needs its own conversation
setting: The team proposes a clinical photograph to document a leg wound.
hook: Elisa is comfortable with examination but stiffens when a camera appears. Her granddaughter recently showed her how quickly family photographs travel through group chats, and she does not want her leg becoming another forwarded image. The learner assumed that agreement to look at the wound covered taking a photograph too. It did not answer Elisa’s question about purpose and handling. The task is to explain the proposed clinical use, follow the local consent process and respect a pause for questions before any image is taken.
question: What should happen before the photograph?
options: Take it quickly to avoid delay
Explain purpose and handling, then clarify consent
Use a personal chat to store it
feedback: The purpose and handling need explanation before the image is taken under the appropriate process. Speed does not replace consent, and an informal personal chat is not an assumed clinical storage route. Elisa’s question is a reasonable request to understand a separate action, not an obstacle to care.
handover: Frau Kern, 62 Jahre, äußert vor geplanter Wundfotodokumentation Fragen zu Zweck und Umgang mit dem Bild. Die Aufnahme erfolgt erst nach Klärung der vorgesehenen Verarbeitung und der erforderlichen Zustimmung.
focus: Explain clinical photography separately from physical examination.

title: A bandage is not a diagnosis
setting: A patient asks to copy a neighbour’s compression treatment.
hook: Otto’s neighbour has a leg ulcer and a firm bandage. Otto has a sore on his own ankle and would like “the same wrapping.” He has even brought a photograph, helpfully annotated with an arrow that says “this bit.” The learner recognises the request but has not assessed his circulation or the cause of his wound. The communication challenge is to explain why the team cannot choose treatment from a matching body part. Otto needs an understandable reason for assessment, not a curt refusal or a copied plan.
question: What must the proposed plan be based on?
options: The neighbour’s photo
The tightest available bandage
Otto’s own wound and circulation assessment
feedback: Otto’s own assessment is the basis for a treatment decision. A neighbour’s photograph does not establish the cause or arterial status, and choosing the tightest bandage is not an appropriate substitute. The learner should explain the purpose of assessment and connect Otto with the trained clinical team.
handover: Herr Voss, 73 Jahre, wünscht bei einer Wunde im Knöchelbereich eine Kompressionsversorgung nach Vorbild seines Nachbarn. Wundursache und arterieller Status sind noch nicht geklärt; die Versorgung wird nach fachlicher Beurteilung geplant.
focus: Explain why wound and arterial assessment precede a compression decision.

title: The dressing room is too loud
setting: A wound review takes place in a noisy treatment area.
hook: Lotte answers yes to several questions, then asks whether the team has said Tuesday or Thursday. Her hearing aid is working, but the trolley wheels, running tap and conversation behind the curtain are winning the competition. The learner nearly interprets her inconsistent answers as poor memory. Lotte is actually trying very hard to follow. The task is to improve communication conditions, face her and check important details in a way she can use. Increasing the volume of medical jargon will not solve the problem.
question: What should change first?
options: The listening conditions and delivery
The patient’s presumed diagnosis
The number of unexplained terms
feedback: Better listening conditions address the evidence in the scene: Lotte cannot distinguish words in the noise. A cognitive diagnosis would be unsupported, and more jargon would add difficulty. Facing her, reducing noise and checking the written date make the plan clearer without treating her as incapable.
handover: Frau Hahn, 68 Jahre, berichtet über Verständnisschwierigkeiten bei Hintergrundgeräuschen trotz Hörgerät. Die Kommunikation wird angepasst und Termininformation schriftlich ergänzt; eine kognitive Beeinträchtigung ist daraus nicht abzuleiten.
focus: Adapt a wound consultation to hearing needs without assuming cognitive impairment.

title: Three dressings, one impossible week
setting: Care planning for repeated wound reviews conflicts with work and transport.
hook: Henrik nods at a plan for repeated visits, then studies the bus timetable on his phone. His shift starts before the first bus reaches the clinic, and a taxi each time would consume his food budget. He has not said no; he has said yes to a plan he cannot carry out. The learner could record “follow-up arranged” and move on. A better conversation checks the journey, work constraints and available services before assuming the timetable on the clinic wall has become a realistic plan in Henrik’s life.
question: What should the record reflect now?
options: All visits successfully arranged
Plan needs transport and scheduling clarification
Patient refuses all wound care
feedback: The plan remains under clarification because the proposed timing is not feasible. Recording it as arranged hides the barrier, while calling it refusal misrepresents Henrik’s willingness. The next useful action is coordination with the service, with the status of that coordination made clear to everyone involved.
handover: Herr Rose, 60 Jahre, kann die vorgeschlagenen Kontrolltermine wegen Busverbindung und Arbeitszeit nach eigenen Angaben nicht erreichen. Nachmittägliche Alternativen werden geprüft; eine durchführbare Terminserie ist noch nicht vereinbart.
focus: Check feasibility of follow-up and distinguish proposed from arranged care.

title: The wound is not the only thing that changed
setting: A routine wound visit becomes an urgent reassessment.
hook: Frieda’s daughter says the dressing has leaked more, but also that her mother has become unusually confused today and feels feverish. Frieda struggles to follow the conversation, which is unlike her usual visits. The learner was preparing a routine progress photograph. The change in general condition now matters more than producing a comparison picture. The task is to recognise the concern, seek urgent clinical assessment and report the daughter’s observations as observations from the daughter, without declaring a confirmed infection source or inventing a measured temperature.
question: What takes priority?
options: The planned photograph
A complete social history
Urgent clinical review of the new confusion
feedback: The new confusion with reported feverishness requires urgent assessment rather than a routine photograph first. A complete social history can wait. The handover should preserve the daughter’s account and uncertainty about the cause, allowing the clinical team to assess the patient rather than inherit an invented diagnosis.
handover: Bei Frau Lang, 75 Jahre, berichtet die Tochter über seit heute neu aufgetretene Verwirrtheit und Fiebergefühl bei vermehrt nässender Wunde. Die Routinekontrolle wird unterbrochen und sofort ärztliche Beurteilung angefordert; Temperatur und Ursache sind noch nicht geklärt.
focus: Escalate a new systemic change and attribute collateral information.

title: The shopping bags can wait
setting: An initial interview reveals ongoing chest pressure with radiation.
hook: Edith carried groceries home because her grandson could not help today. She now describes pressure behind the breastbone, spreading toward her jaw and left arm, with nausea. She asks whether she should first explain her usual tablets. The learner has enough information to be concerned but no examination or test results. This is not a moment for a complete rehearsed admission interview. The task is to stop the routine sequence, summon the clinical team immediately and explain the urgency in clear language without announcing a confirmed heart attack.
question: What should the learner do first?
options: Complete the standard interview
Call the clinical team immediately
Promise it is indigestion
feedback: Immediate escalation fits the potentially serious symptom combination. Completing the standard interview would delay assessment, while reassurance about indigestion would invent a cause. The handover should state the reported symptoms and concern, with unknown findings left unknown rather than filled in to make the presentation sound complete.
handover: Frau Weller, 76 Jahre, berichtet über anhaltenden retrosternalen Druck mit Ausstrahlung in Unterkiefer und linken Arm sowie Übelkeit. Bei möglichem ACS wird das Gespräch unterbrochen und sofort das ärztliche Team angefordert; Vitalparameter und EKG liegen noch nicht vor.
focus: Interrupt routine history when symptoms suggest a possible acute coronary syndrome.

title: Half an hour since what?
setting: A focused symptom clarification occurs while the emergency team responds.
hook: Lukas says the pain started half an hour ago. A moment later he explains that mild pressure began at breakfast, became worse at work and led him to call for help half an hour ago. The clinical team has already been summoned. The learner has a brief chance to clarify the timeline without delaying assessment. Several clocks are hiding in one answer: first symptom, worsening and decision to seek help. The goal is an accurate account of what Lukas remembers, not a forced exact minute chosen because it sounds tidy.
question: Which timeline should be handed over?
options: Only the call time
An invented exact minute
Mild pressure at breakfast, marked worsening later
feedback: The two-stage timeline preserves Lukas’s meaning. Using only the call time erases earlier symptoms, while choosing an exact minute he cannot recall creates false accuracy. The clarification remains brief because the clinical response is already underway and must not wait for a polished chronological narrative.
handover: Herr Sander, 48 Jahre, berichtet über zunächst leichten Brustdruck seit dem Frühstück mit deutlicher Zunahme etwa vor einer halben Stunde. Das ärztliche Team ist bereits angefordert; genaue Uhrzeiten und Befunde sind noch offen.
focus: Clarify symptom onset separately from the call for help during escalation.

title: Will I die? deserves an honest sentence
setting: A frightened patient awaits urgent assessment for chest symptoms.
hook: Miriam asks, “Am I going to die?” The question arrives while the urgent clinical response is already being arranged. The learner wants to comfort her and feels the pull of saying “No, of course not.” But no one has established the cause or prognosis. Miriam needs presence and a clear next step, not a promise made to reduce the clinician’s discomfort. The communication task is to acknowledge the fear, explain what is happening now and remain truthful while the team assesses the possible emergency.
question: Which response is both caring and honest?
options: Name the fear and explain the urgent response
Guarantee survival
Ignore the question until all results return
feedback: Naming the fear and explaining the response gives support without inventing an outcome. A survival guarantee exceeds the information available, while ignoring the question leaves Miriam alone with it. The learner can be brief and compassionate even during escalation, with the urgent assessment remaining the priority.
handover: Frau West, 63 Jahre, äußert bei akut abzuklärenden Brustbeschwerden ausgeprägte Todesangst. Die dringende ärztliche Beurteilung ist veranlasst; Ursache und Prognose sind noch nicht geklärt.
focus: Respond to fear without guaranteeing safety or outcome.

title: The wires need a sentence
setting: The team prepares an ECG during urgent chest-pain assessment.
hook: Armin sees adhesive electrodes and asks whether the machine will send electricity into his heart. The clinical team is already assessing him, and nobody needs a long physics lecture. The learner can give a brief, accurate explanation while supporting the urgent process. Armin is not refusing; he is trying to understand unfamiliar equipment at a frightening moment. The task is to explain what an ECG records, preserve dignity while the chest is accessed, and avoid implying that one test will automatically answer every question about his pain.
question: Which sentence answers Armin’s actual concern?
options: The test guarantees a normal heart
It records signals rather than giving a shock
You need not understand it
feedback: The recording-versus-shock distinction directly addresses Armin’s fear. A promise about a normal heart confuses the procedure with an unknown result, while dismissing the question undermines participation. A concise explanation can fit into urgent assessment without turning it into a lengthy lesson or delaying the team.
handover: Herr Koch, 57 Jahre, wird bei Brustbeschwerden akut beurteilt; ein EKG wird vorbereitet. Seine Sorge vor einem Stromschlag wurde durch Erklärung der Signalaufzeichnung adressiert; ein EKG-Befund liegt noch nicht vor.
focus: Give a short procedure explanation during urgent care.

title: One result is not the whole conversation
setting: During ongoing assessment, a patient overinterprets an initial update.
hook: Sabine hears that an initial investigation has not shown a clear answer. She translates this into “nothing is wrong” and begins messaging her family that she can leave. The clinician has not yet completed the assessment, and the learner does not have authority to reinterpret the result as an all-clear. This is a common communication gap: the team is describing uncertainty while the patient hears reassurance. The task is to repeat the actual status, explain that the overall assessment continues and ask the treating team to clarify the next step.
question: What should be clarified?
options: That every initial result is useless
That she can leave now
That assessment remains ongoing
feedback: The important correction is the status of the assessment. The initial information may be useful without being final. Calling it useless exaggerates in the other direction, and suggesting departure invents a decision. The treating team should explain what remains open and what happens next.
handover: Frau Roth, 65 Jahre, interpretiert eine erste nicht abschließende Untersuchungsinformation als Entwarnung. Die Abklärung der Brustbeschwerden ist noch nicht abgeschlossen; eine Erläuterung des weiteren Vorgehens durch das Behandlungsteam wird veranlasst.
focus: Prevent an inconclusive initial result from becoming a false all-clear.

title: The front-door keys are already in her hand
setting: A patient wants to leave while urgent chest-pain assessment is incomplete.
hook: Dora reaches for her keys and says she cannot stay. Her dog is alone, her phone battery is almost empty and she thinks signing a form will settle the matter. The learner must not reduce the situation to a signature or promise that nothing will happen if she leaves. Urgent assessment is still needed. The task is to explore the practical reason, explain the concern clearly and involve the responsible clinician promptly, supporting an informed discussion rather than using either pressure or paperwork as a substitute for communication.
question: What is the best immediate response?
options: Explore the barrier and involve the responsible clinician
Treat the signature as the entire process
Hide her keys
feedback: The practical barrier and clinical concern both need attention. A signature alone does not establish an informed discussion, while hiding keys is coercive and does not solve the communication problem. The responsible clinician should promptly address the unresolved risk and decision-making situation with Dora.
handover: Frau Neumann, 71 Jahre, möchte die noch nicht abgeschlossene Abklärung von Brustbeschwerden wegen eines allein zu Hause befindlichen Hundes verlassen. Die verantwortliche Ärztin wird umgehend zum Risiko- und Entscheidungsgespräch hinzugezogen; eine Versorgung des Tieres ist noch nicht organisiert.
focus: Respond to intended departure during unresolved urgent assessment.

title: The family update has a boundary
setting: After urgent escalation, a relative calls asking for a diagnosis.
hook: Nadia’s adult son calls the desk while the team is assessing her chest symptoms. He asks whether she has had a heart attack and whether he should tell the whole family. Nadia is able to express her preferences and wants her daughter contacted first. The learner feels pressure to provide a useful answer quickly. The task is to respect Nadia’s wishes, follow the appropriate identity and disclosure process, and avoid upgrading a suspected diagnosis into confirmed news merely because a worried relative wants a clear headline.
question: What should guide the update?
options: The loudest caller’s request
Nadia’s preferences and the verified clinical status
A dramatic diagnosis to make the family come
feedback: Nadia’s wishes and the actual assessment status guide the communication within the appropriate process. A demanding caller does not automatically determine access, and inventing a dramatic diagnosis distorts the information. Urgency can be communicated honestly without turning a possible cause into confirmed news.
handover: Frau Sturm, 60 Jahre, wird wegen Brustbeschwerden dringend untersucht und wünscht zunächst Kontakt zur Tochter. Eine Diagnose ist noch nicht gesichert; Umfang und Empfänger der Information werden mit der Patientin abgestimmt.
focus: Combine patient preferences and diagnostic uncertainty in a family update.

title: The handover starts with why you called
setting: A learner hands over to the arriving clinical team.
hook: Peter has chest pressure and sweating. The learner has called the clinical team and now begins the handover with his occupation, marital status and childhood operation. The information may belong somewhere in a full history, but it is hiding the reason the team came urgently. Peter is listening and wants to know that the new symptoms have been understood. The task is to lead with the immediate problem, timing and concern, distinguish reported symptoms from observations, and state which important measurements or facts are still unavailable.
question: What belongs in the first sentence?
options: Childhood operation
