Occupation and number of children
Ongoing chest pressure and urgent concern
feedback: The first sentence should explain why the team was called. Biography and remote history can follow if relevant. The learner should not invent normal vital signs to make the summary sound complete; stating that measurements are not yet available is clearer and safer for the receiving team.
handover: Herr Hahn, 67 Jahre, berichtet über aktuell anhaltenden Brustdruck und Schwitzen; deshalb wurde sofort das ärztliche Team angefordert. Beginn, Vitalparameter und EKG-Befund sind noch nicht vollständig erhoben beziehungsweise verfügbar.
focus: Lead an urgent handover with the immediate problem and explicit unknowns.

title: The pillows have quietly multiplied
setting: A consultation explores breathlessness and changed sleep posture.
hook: Konstanze says she sleeps badly. The trainee nearly opens the standard insomnia questions, but her daughter mentions that the bed now contains four pillows where there used to be one. Konstanze laughs gently that the cushions are taking over the household, then explains that lying flat makes her breathing uncomfortable. She had not thought of this as a breathing symptom because it happens at bedtime. The task is to ask what the pillows are doing for her, clarify the change and arrange clinical assessment rather than treating every disrupted night as ordinary insomnia.
question: Which follow-up uncovers the meaning of the pillows?
options: Ask why lying flatter is difficult
Count cushions as a diagnosis
Recommend a sleeping tablet immediately
feedback: Asking what changes when she lies flat uncovers the breathing symptom and its timeline. Pillows alone do not establish a diagnosis, and a sleep-medication suggestion skips the actual concern. The learner should use the information to support clinical assessment, with immediate escalation if severe breathing difficulty is present.
handover: Frau Adler, 64 Jahre, berichtet über neu erhöhten Kissenbedarf wegen Atemnot in flacher Liegeposition. Beginn, Verlauf und aktueller Schweregrad werden geklärt; eine kardiale Ursache ist möglich, aber nicht bestätigt.
focus: Uncover breathlessness when lying flat through a practical sleep question.

title: The first floor used to be the warm-up
setting: A history focuses on declining exercise tolerance.
hook: Monika lives on the fourth floor. She says she is “a little slower,” which sounds mild until she explains that she now stops on the first landing to catch her breath. Last month she could reach her door without stopping. She jokes that the stairs have added extra steps when nobody was watching. The learner needs her previous and current ability, the timescale and any symptoms at rest. The building’s floor number alone does not explain what changed, and a social-history box will not capture the functional loss.
question: Which comparison is most informative?
options: Her floor versus the neighbour’s floor
The same stairs now versus last month
Her shoe size over time
feedback: The same activity at two points in time shows a meaningful functional change. Comparing neighbours introduces different bodies and habits, while shoe size does not answer the question. The learner should preserve Monika’s report and arrange assessment rather than infer a cause from the comparison alone.
handover: Frau Hess, 61 Jahre, berichtet über zunehmende Belastungsdyspnoe: aktuell Pause im ersten Stock, vor einem Monat Aufstieg bis zum vierten Stock ohne Pause. Angaben zu Ruhesymptomen und objektive Befunde fehlen noch.
focus: Compare current function with the patient’s own baseline.

title: The scale is not accusing anyone
setting: A review explores weight change alongside ankle swelling.
hook: Rudi has gained weight over a short period and apologises for eating cake at a family celebration. His shoes also feel tighter, and he has noticed swollen ankles. The learner should not assume either that cake explains everything or that fluid retention is already proven. Rudi expects a lecture about willpower; the useful conversation is about dates, measurements, swelling and breathing. The scale is a source of information, not a moral judge, and the patient’s account needs assessment before a cause or a treatment change is announced.
question: What should the learner avoid?
options: Asking about the dates
Recording the ankle change
Assuming cake or fluid is the proven cause
feedback: The learner should avoid a proven-cause claim in either direction. Dates and associated ankle changes are useful information, but neither establishes why the weight changed. Clinical review can interpret the pattern; the conversation should gather it accurately without a blame narrative or an improvised treatment adjustment.
handover: Herr Klein, 68 Jahre, berichtet über Gewichtszunahme und dickere Knöchel seit einigen Tagen. Verlässliche Vergleichsmessungen fehlen; Ursache und begleitende Symptome werden ärztlich abgeklärt.
focus: Discuss weight gain and swelling without blame or premature attribution.

title: The word failure landed badly
setting: A clinician has discussed possible heart failure and the patient asks what it means.
hook: Anja has heard “heart failure” and thinks her heart has stopped, or will stop at any moment. The learner notices that she has stopped listening to everything after those two words. She is an accountant who likes definitions, but this label sounds final rather than descriptive. The task is to explain the term gently, distinguish a pumping problem from a stopped heart and preserve the fact that her own diagnosis is still being assessed. A clearer explanation should reduce misunderstanding without minimising the seriousness of a possible condition.
question: Which distinction should the explanation make?
options: Meaning of the term versus whether Anja has it
A serious word means a certain diagnosis
Failure means the heart has stopped
feedback: The explanation needs both a plain definition and the status of Anja’s assessment. A frightening word is not diagnostic proof, and heart failure does not mean the heart has stopped. Clear language should remove that misunderstanding while keeping the need for assessment and the possible seriousness visible.
handover: Frau Bergmann, 59 Jahre, fragt nach der Bedeutung des geäußerten Verdachts auf Herzinsuffizienz. Der Begriff wurde erläutert; eine gesicherte Diagnose und eine individuelle Prognose liegen noch nicht vor.
focus: Explain an alarming disease label without minimising uncertainty or seriousness.

title: The internet gave everyone the same bottle
setting: A patient asks about fluid instructions found online.
hook: Felix arrives with a large water bottle and two contradictory printouts. One website says to drink generously; another appears to demand strict restriction. He has written both instructions on sticky notes, which now argue silently on the bottle. His clinician is assessing possible heart failure, but no individual fluid plan has been discussed in this scene. The learner should not settle the argument with a generic number. The task is to identify the current advice, explain that recommendations depend on the clinical situation and arrange clarification with the treating team.
question: What should resolve the conflicting numbers?
options: The strictest number online
An individual instruction from the treating team
The bottle’s maximum capacity
feedback: An individual instruction from the treating team addresses Felix’s actual situation. The strictest online rule is not automatically appropriate, and bottle size is packaging rather than clinical advice. The learner should clarify existing instructions and support understanding without inventing a fluid prescription.
handover: Herr Horn, 66 Jahre, ist wegen widersprüchlicher allgemeiner Trinkmengenangaben verunsichert. Eine individuelle Flüssigkeitsempfehlung ist in dieser Szene nicht bekannt und wird mit dem Behandlungsteam geklärt; eine pauschale Restriktion wird nicht vorgegeben.
focus: Decline generic fluid prescriptions and clarify an individual plan.

title: The tablet and the bus timetable
setting: A medication review explores missed prescribed doses without changing treatment.
hook: Ilse admits skipping a prescribed water tablet on days when she travels by bus. The journey has no convenient toilet stop, and the clinic appointment often adds a long wait. She says this quietly, expecting to be told off. The learner could label her unreliable or suggest a new schedule on the spot. A better conversation identifies the real barrier, clarifies the medicine and current instructions, and asks the prescribing team to review a practical plan. The bus timetable belongs in this history because it changes what actually happens.
question: What is the most useful next step?
options: Call her unreliable
Invent a replacement schedule
Clarify actual use and seek prescribing review
feedback: Clarifying actual use and the barrier gives the prescribing team something actionable to review. Blame may conceal future omissions, while a new schedule without assessment creates another unverified instruction. The record should preserve both the intended plan and Ilse’s reported pattern of use.
handover: Frau Brand, 74 Jahre, berichtet, ein als Wassertablette bezeichnetes Medikament an Busreisetagen gelegentlich auszulassen. Präparat und Einnahmeplan sind zu verifizieren; die fehlende Toilettenmöglichkeit wird zur ärztlichen Therapieprüfung weitergegeben.
focus: Explore medication omission caused by daily-life constraints.

title: Breathlessness is not waiting for morning
setting: A patient becomes markedly breathless during a planned review.
hook: Tariq arrived to discuss several weeks of increasing breathlessness. During the conversation he becomes much more short of breath and can manage only a few words at a time. He asks whether he should keep describing his night-time symptoms. The learner has not established the cause and must not assume this is merely the familiar pattern. The routine review must stop. The task is to summon the clinical team immediately, communicate the observed change and use brief reassuring explanations about action rather than promises about the outcome.
question: What determines the immediate priority?
options: The new severe breathing difficulty
The age of the original complaint
The remaining form questions
feedback: The new severe difficulty determines the priority and requires immediate clinical help. A weeks-long background does not make today’s deterioration routine. The handover should distinguish the observed difficulty speaking from unmeasured vital signs, so the team receives clear facts instead of a guessed explanation.
handover: Herr Keller, 70 Jahre, berichtet über länger zunehmende Dyspnoe und zeigt im Gespräch eine deutliche akute Verschlechterung mit nur kurzen Sprechabschnitten. Sofortige ärztliche Unterstützung wird angefordert; Vitalparameter und Ursache sind noch nicht bekannt.
focus: Recognise and communicate acute deterioration during a chronic-symptom review.

title: The plan has to reach the fourth floor
setting: The team discusses a possible future home plan after assessment.
hook: Erika’s draft plan says “home with follow-up.” It sounds pleasantly complete until she asks how she will reach her fourth-floor flat while the lift is being repaired. Her daughter can bring shopping on Sundays but cannot stay during the week. Nobody has made a discharge decision in this scene; they are checking what a future plan would require. The learner must turn broad words into practical questions without promising transport or home services that have not been arranged. A plan should travel farther than the printer tray.
question: Which status is accurate?
options: All home support confirmed
Practical gaps remain in a proposed plan
Discharge is impossible forever
feedback: The scene establishes practical gaps, not a completed arrangement or a permanent impossibility. Stating them clearly lets the team explore options. The learner should avoid promising a service or announcing a discharge decision that has not been made, while ensuring Erika’s actual living situation is heard.
handover: Frau Lenz, 69 Jahre, berichtet über eine Wohnung im vierten Stock bei defektem Aufzug; Hilfe durch die Tochter sei nur sonntags verfügbar. Diese Versorgungslücken werden in die weitere Planung eingebracht; eine Entlassungsentscheidung ist hier noch nicht getroffen.
focus: Translate a proposed home plan into verified practical arrangements.

title: The bouquet can wait; the breathing cannot
setting: A florist attends with feverishness, cough and difficulty breathing.
hook: Flora arrived thinking she needed something for a stubborn cough before a busy wedding weekend. During the first questions, she becomes markedly breathless and struggles to finish a sentence. The learner has heard about yellow sputum but has no measured temperature, oxygen reading or chest findings. The order of the conversation must change. This is not a chance to finish the occupational history or debate whether the sputum proves a bacterial infection. The task is to stop, summon the clinical team and communicate the immediate breathing difficulty accurately.
question: What comes first?
options: A complete flower-exposure history
A sputum-colour diagnosis
Immediate clinical help for breathing difficulty
feedback: Immediate help addresses the severe current breathing problem. Workplace exposures can be explored later, and sputum colour cannot carry the whole diagnosis. The learner should pass on the actual symptoms and observation, making clear which measurements are still unavailable rather than inventing normal or abnormal values.
handover: Frau Neumann, 46 Jahre, berichtet über Husten mit gelblichem Auswurf und zeigt ausgeprägte Atemnot mit erschwertem Sprechen. Das Gespräch wird unterbrochen und sofort klinische Unterstützung angefordert; Vitalparameter und Auskultationsbefund liegen noch nicht vor.
focus: Prioritise severe breathing difficulty over a complete infection history.

title: The thermometer was never consulted
setting: A history distinguishes feeling feverish from a measured fever.
hook: Bastian says he had a temperature of “about forty.” The learner looks up sharply. Bastian then admits he never used a thermometer; he felt hot under two blankets while shivering. His household thermometer is somewhere in the drawer that also contains expired batteries and a mysterious key. The report still matters, but the number is an estimate, not a measurement. The task is to clarify what he experienced and what was measured without embarrassing him or discarding the symptom because the instrument was not available.
question: Which entry respects both symptom and uncertainty?
options: Feverishness reported; no measured temperature
No fever because no thermometer
Measured forty degrees
feedback: The correct entry keeps Bastian’s experience and the absence of a measurement. Saying no fever would go beyond the information just as much as recording forty degrees as measured. The conversation should clarify the symptom pattern without converting an estimate into either a proven value or a negative finding.
handover: Herr Roth, 35 Jahre, berichtet über Fiebergefühl und Zittern, hat die Temperatur jedoch nicht gemessen. Die zunächst genannte Angabe von etwa 40 Grad war eine Schätzung; aktuelle Vitalparameter fehlen noch.
focus: Distinguish subjective feverishness from measured temperature.

title: The colour chart cannot choose an antibiotic
setting: A patient expects antibiotics because her sputum looks green.
hook: Katja has photographed her sputum because a friend said green means bacteria. She arrives expecting a particular antibiotic and has scheduled the consultation as a quick stop between errands. The learner can acknowledge her effort to describe the change without treating the photograph as a prescription request that must be fulfilled. The colour is one part of the history, not a complete explanation. The task is to ask about the whole illness, explain the need for assessment and avoid both automatic antibiotics and a dismissive “it is only a cold.”
question: What is the useful reply?
options: The photo proves the pathogen
Colour alone does not decide; assess the whole illness
Ignore her observation completely
feedback: The colour is worth recording, but it cannot make the treatment decision by itself. Calling it proof overstates the evidence, while ignoring it dismisses Katja’s attempt to help. Explaining the wider assessment offers a practical reason for further questions without giving a premature diagnosis or prescription.
handover: Frau Frank, 43 Jahre, berichtet über grünlichen Auswurf und erwartet eine antibiotische Behandlung. Verlauf, Begleitsymptome und Untersuchungsbefunde sind noch zu erheben; aus der Farbe allein wird keine Therapieentscheidung abgeleitet.
focus: Address an antibiotic expectation without diagnosing from sputum colour.

title: Swallowing is the question now
setting: A sore-throat consultation reveals inability to swallow saliva.
hook: Anika came expecting a discussion about tonsils and a certificate for work. She now says she cannot swallow her saliva and has increasing difficulty breathing. The learner has not looked in her throat and must not decide that this is an uncomplicated sore throat from the appointment label. The task is immediate escalation, not finishing the symptom checklist. Anika needs short instructions and urgent clinical assessment; there is no place here for a joke about losing her voice or a promise that a routine tablet will solve it.
question: What should replace the routine sore-throat interview?
options: A work-certificate discussion
A promise of quick antibiotic relief
Immediate clinical escalation
feedback: Immediate escalation responds to the reported inability to swallow saliva and worsening breathing. Employment paperwork can wait, and a treatment promise skips the urgent assessment. The learner should state the symptoms and concern while leaving the specific cause open for the clinical team to establish.
handover: Frau Wolf, 28 Jahre, berichtet bei Halsschmerzen über fehlende Schluckfähigkeit für Speichel und zunehmende Atemnot. Das Gespräch wird sofort unterbrochen und klinische Unterstützung angefordert; eine genaue Ursache ist noch nicht festgestellt.
focus: Escalate airway-related warning symptoms in a sore-throat presentation.

title: Blood from where?
setting: A patient reports blood seen during a respiratory illness.
hook: Nils says there was blood when he coughed. He also had a nosebleed earlier, and he is unsure whether the blood came from his chest, nose or mouth. The learner is tempted to choose one explanation quickly so the history can move on. Nils has already searched three frightening phrases online and wants certainty. The task is to clarify what he actually saw, assess urgency with the clinical team and preserve uncertainty about the source, rather than declaring either a harmless nosebleed or a confirmed lung bleed.
question: Which summary matches the available information?
options: Blood reported; source uncertain after nosebleed and cough
Confirmed harmless nasal source
Confirmed lung bleeding
feedback: The source remains uncertain and should be described that way. Both definitive alternatives add information not established in the conversation. Clarifying the sequence and obtaining clinical assessment can guide the next step, while urgent features must prompt escalation rather than a prolonged attempt to solve the source verbally.
handover: Herr Weber, 54 Jahre, berichtet über Blutbeimengung im Zusammenhang mit Husten sowie vorausgegangene Epistaxis. Die Blutungsquelle ist unklar; Menge, aktueller Verlauf und respiratorischer Zustand werden zeitnah beurteilt.
focus: Clarify an ambiguous bleeding report without dismissing it.

title: A picture with a purpose
setting: A patient asks why a chest X-ray has been proposed.
hook: Jana thought listening with a stethoscope would finish the consultation. When the clinician proposes a chest X-ray, she worries that the team has found something terrible but is not telling her. Her mind has supplied an entire plot between two ordinary sentences. The learner’s job is to explain the purpose of the proposed investigation, invite her specific concern and avoid saying it is harmless or guaranteed to show the answer. The decision belongs in a conversation about why the test is useful in her situation, not in a mysterious trip down a corridor.
question: What is the clearest explanation?
options: The order proves pneumonia
The image helps investigate a specific question
There are no risks or limitations
feedback: Explaining the diagnostic question gives Jana a reason for the proposed image without announcing its result. An order does not prove pneumonia, and absolute claims about risks or limitations are not justified. Her concerns should be addressed as part of the discussion with the responsible clinical team.
handover: Frau Beck, 39 Jahre, fragt nach dem Zweck einer vorgeschlagenen Röntgenaufnahme des Thorax. Die diagnostische Fragestellung wird erläutert; ein Bildbefund oder eine gesicherte Pneumonie ist in dieser Szene nicht vorhanden.
focus: Explain an investigation as a question being explored, not proof of a feared diagnosis.

title: The certificate cannot predict Friday
setting: A patient with a respiratory illness asks for a guaranteed return-to-work date.
hook: Dario has a shift rota, a coughing colleague and a manager who likes definite dates. He asks whether he can promise to return on Friday before the assessment is complete. The learner wants to help and could offer a cheerful estimate as if it were a guarantee. Dario’s real need is a way to communicate uncertainty to work without seeming unreliable. The task is to explain that recovery and fitness decisions depend on assessment and progress, then clarify the appropriate documentation process without inventing an outcome for the employer’s spreadsheet.
question: What can the learner responsibly offer?
options: A guaranteed Friday recovery
A diagnosis sent to the whole workplace
A clear assessment status and documentation discussion
feedback: The learner can clarify the current status and documentation process. A guaranteed recovery date is unsupported, and broad diagnostic sharing is not an automatic part of workplace communication. Dario’s need for a practical message can be met without converting uncertainty into a promise.
handover: Herr Lang, 31 Jahre, fragt bei noch laufender Abklärung eines Atemwegsinfekts nach einer sicheren Arbeitsaufnahme am Freitag. Eine verlässliche Prognose liegt noch nicht vor; Bescheinigung und weitere Rückmeldung werden mit dem Behandlungsteam geklärt.
focus: Discuss work expectations without guaranteeing recovery or unnecessary disclosure.

title: The leaflet is not the last word
setting: After assessment, a learner checks understanding of the team’s actual follow-up advice.
hook: Vera has received a written plan from the treating clinician, but she can explain only the first line. The rest contains contact details, follow-up information and instructions about worsening symptoms. She folded it carefully, which made it look understood. Her handbag now contains a very organised uncertainty. The learner should not invent a new discharge plan or assume the leaflet has done the teaching. The task is to review the actual instructions with her, check how she would seek help and bring any unanswered clinical questions back to the responsible team.
question: What is the best understanding check?
options: Ask how she would use the actual plan if worse
Ask whether the leaflet is folded neatly
Create a different contact route from memory
feedback: A concrete “what would you do?” check shows whether Vera can use the plan. Neat paperwork says nothing about understanding, and a new route from memory may conflict with the clinician’s instructions. Any missing or unclear advice should be clarified with the responsible team before relying on the plan.
handover: Frau Stahl, 58 Jahre, hat Rückfragen zu einem bereits ausgehändigten Behandlungs- und Kontaktplan. Die bestehenden Angaben werden gemeinsam geprüft und offene Fragen dem verantwortlichen Team vorgelegt; zusätzliche klinische Anweisungen werden hier nicht erfunden.
focus: Check usable understanding of an existing plan without creating a new one.

title: The night-time whistle nobody invited
setting: A daytime consultation explores intermittent night-time respiratory symptoms.
hook: Ferdinand feels fairly comfortable in the consultation room and worries that this will make his night-time symptoms sound imaginary. For two weeks he has woken coughing, sometimes with a whistle on breathing out. His partner first blamed the bedroom window, which has an impressive repertoire of noises of its own. The learner must ask about the episodes rather than assume that a calm daytime conversation rules them out. The useful history includes timing, frequency, associated tightness and what he does when it happens, without declaring asthma from a single description.
question: What should the learner do with the night-time account?
options: Dismiss it because he is comfortable now
Explore and record the intermittent pattern
Confirm asthma without assessment
feedback: Exploring the pattern respects the report without overclaiming its cause. Dismissing it confuses the current moment with the whole illness; confirming asthma skips assessment. The handover should say that night-time coughing and wheeze are reported, while examination and any diagnostic testing remain separate sources of information.
handover: Herr Nord, 34 Jahre, berichtet über seit zwei Wochen wiederkehrenden nächtlichen Husten und pfeifende Exspiration, mehrmals wöchentlich mit Erwachen. Aktuell beschreibt er eine Besserung; objektive Befunde und Diagnose sind noch offen.
focus: Take intermittent symptoms seriously when they are absent during the visit.

title: Show me is kinder than do you know
setting: A routine review checks use of an already prescribed inhaler.
hook: Lina says she knows how to use her inhaler because someone explained it quickly at the pharmacy. She is less certain when asked to describe the steps. The device came with a leaflet, a box and enough small print to wallpaper a doll’s house. The learner should not quiz her from memory or demonstrate a generic technique for an unidentified device. The task is to identify the actual inhaler, invite a demonstration with an appropriate training device and arrange device-specific coaching with the responsible professional.
question: What is the best way to check technique?
options: A memory quiz with no device
One technique for every inhaler
Identify the device and invite a supported demonstration
feedback: The actual device and a supported demonstration make the review practical. A memory quiz can miss a physical technique problem, while one generic method may be unsuitable. The goal is to improve confidence and use of the prescribed device, with coaching from an appropriately trained professional.
handover: Frau Berg, 26 Jahre, äußert Unsicherheit bei der Anwendung ihres verordneten Inhalators. Präparat und Gerät werden zunächst identifiziert; eine gerätespezifische Anwendungskontrolle mit angeleiteter Rückdemonstration ist vorgesehen.
focus: Use demonstration to review device technique without shaming or assuming a device type.

title: The workshop might be a clue
setting: A symptom history includes possible workplace triggers.
hook: Tobias repairs furniture and notices more coughing on workshop days. He worries that mentioning dust will cost him his livelihood, so he first says only that he has “a bit of a cough.” On weekends it sometimes improves, but he has not tracked it carefully. The learner should explore the pattern without announcing that work definitely caused asthma or promising that nothing will need to change. The task is to gather useful exposure and timing information while acknowledging why the question feels bigger than a simple item on a form.
question: What should the learner establish first?
options: The pattern of tasks, exposure and symptoms
A guaranteed job-change decision
A promise that work is irrelevant
feedback: The pattern is the useful first step. Neither an immediate job-change decision nor a promise of irrelevance is justified by the current account. Tobias can be reassured that describing his experience is not the same as accepting a predetermined conclusion, while the possible clinical relevance remains clear.
handover: Herr Braun, 42 Jahre, berichtet über vermehrten Husten an Werkstatttagen mit Staubkontakt und teilweise Besserung an freien Tagen. Ein arbeitsbezogener Zusammenhang ist möglich, aber nicht gesichert; weitere Anamnese und Diagnostik stehen aus.
focus: Explore a suspected occupational pattern without asserting causation.

title: Fear and breathing can share the room
setting: A patient with respiratory episodes also describes recent emotional stress.
hook: Amir has been under severe stress since a family loss. He also reports recurrent chest tightness and wheezing. When he mentions panic during an episode, the learner is tempted to decide the problem is “just anxiety.” Amir fears that talking about grief has made the breathing complaint less believable. The communication task is to acknowledge the emotional context while keeping physical assessment open. If significant breathing difficulty is present now, urgent help takes priority; if not, both the episodes and the distress deserve careful, unhurried clarification.
question: What is the best approach?
options: Treat grief as proof of the cause
Assess breathing and distress without dismissing either
Refuse to discuss emotions
feedback: Both threads deserve attention, with urgent breathing needs taking priority if present. Grief is not proof that the respiratory symptoms are psychological, while refusing emotional discussion ignores part of Amir’s experience. The learner should clarify the sequence and keep diagnostic possibilities open for proper assessment.
handover: Herr Seidel, 33 Jahre, berichtet über episodische Brustenge und Giemen mit Angst während der Episoden sowie erhebliche seelische Belastung. Eine allein psychische Ursache ist nicht belegt; aktueller respiratorischer Zustand und weitere Befunde werden erhoben.
focus: Avoid attributing respiratory symptoms solely to anxiety after hearing an emotional context.

title: The breathing test is not a competition
setting: A patient prepares for a proposed lung-function assessment.
hook: Ella hears that she will blow into a device and assumes the aim is to beat a target. She asks whether being bad at sport means she will fail. The learner notices that “test” has sounded like an exam rather than a measurement. The conversation should explain the purpose of lung-function assessment, the role of coached technique and the fact that staff will guide the process. Ella does not need a pep talk about winning or a promise that one attempt will establish her diagnosis. She needs permission to ask and try again if instructed.
question: What should Ella understand?
options: The strongest person wins
A low value means poor effort automatically
The team guides a measurement, not an exam
feedback: The guided-measurement explanation removes an unhelpful competition. A value cannot automatically be blamed on effort, and the patient is not trying to defeat someone else’s score. Trained staff guide technique and interpretation, while the learner helps Ella understand the purpose and ask questions.
handover: Frau Fuchs, 24 Jahre, äußert Leistungsangst vor einer vorgeschlagenen Spirometrie. Zweck und angeleiteter Ablauf werden erläutert; Messwerte, Durchführbarkeit und diagnostische Einordnung liegen noch nicht vor.
focus: Explain a cooperative diagnostic task without performance judgement.

title: The blue one is not a complete treatment history
setting: A review reveals uncertainty about prescribed inhaler roles.
hook: Malte owns two inhalers and identifies them only by colour. One lives beside the kettle and the other in a coat he rarely wears. He has read advice about preventers and relievers, but he is unsure which terms apply to his actual prescription. The learner must not map colour automatically to a modern regimen or recite a remembered treatment ladder. The task is to identify the devices and medicines, clarify the current written plan and ask the treating team to explain the role of each in Malte’s own care.
question: What should determine the explanation of each inhaler?
options: Exact product and current individual plan
Colour alone
A treatment ladder remembered from years ago
feedback: The exact products and current plan determine what Malte needs to understand. Colour alone can mislead, and a remembered scheme may not match his prescription. The learner’s contribution is reconciliation and clear explanation with the responsible team, not an independently invented regimen.
handover: Herr Horn, 45 Jahre, kann zwei Inhalatoren nur nach Farbe unterscheiden und ist über die Anwendung unsicher. Präparate, aktueller Therapieplan und tatsächliche Nutzung werden abgeglichen; eine neue Dosierungsanweisung wird hier nicht gegeben.
focus: Clarify inhaler roles from the actual prescription rather than colour stereotypes.

title: The explanation pauses when breathing worsens
setting: An inhaler review is interrupted by rapidly worsening breathlessness.
hook: Sara is discussing her existing asthma plan when her breathing becomes much worse. She cannot complete her answers and says her usual help has not improved the symptoms. The learner has the plan in front of them but has not verified the exact medicine or measured her condition. This is not a moment to keep teaching inhaler technique or improvise doses from a generic memory. The routine discussion stops, the clinical team is summoned immediately and the key facts about worsening symptoms and reported treatment response are handed over.
question: What takes priority over inhaler teaching?
options: A perfect demonstration
Immediate clinical escalation
A general dosing rule from memory
feedback: Immediate escalation responds to the worsening breathing difficulty and reported lack of improvement. A demonstration would delay the response, and generic dosing from memory may not fit the actual medicine or plan. The learner should communicate the change and make the available plan accessible to the treating team.
handover: Frau Lind, 30 Jahre, entwickelt bei bekannter Asthmaanamnese zunehmende Atemnot mit erschwertem Sprechen und berichtet über fehlende Besserung nach ihrem üblichen Mittel. Sofortige klinische Hilfe wird angefordert; Präparat, Anwendung und Vitalparameter sind noch zu verifizieren.
focus: Escalate a worsening respiratory episode rather than continue education.

title: A diary with useful blanks
setting: A clinician suggests recording episodes to clarify an intermittent pattern.
hook: Clara wants to help explain her intermittent cough, so she has created a spreadsheet with twenty columns. By day two it feels like a second job, complete with disappointing management. The learner can help her understand the purpose of a simple symptom record without asking her to diagnose herself or fill unknown values. The useful entries are concrete observations: when symptoms happen, what she was doing, and what she used under her existing plan. Missing entries should stay missing, and urgent symptoms should prompt help rather than a carefully completed row.
question: What makes the diary useful?
options: Every box filled with guesses
A diagnosis written after each cough
A few reliable observations with uncertainty marked
feedback: Reliable observations help clarify a pattern even when some entries are missing. Guesses create false detail, and a diagnosis after each episode goes beyond the diary’s role. Clara should understand both what to record and that urgent symptoms take priority over completing the record.
handover: Frau Jung, 36 Jahre, möchte intermittierende Atemwegsbeschwerden dokumentieren und berichtet über Schwierigkeiten mit einer umfangreichen Tabelle. Ein praktikables Beobachtungsschema wird mit dem Team abgestimmt; unklare Angaben bleiben gekennzeichnet und ersetzen keine klinische Beurteilung.
focus: Make symptom tracking practical and separate observation from diagnosis.

title: The soup menu nobody ordered
setting: Jonas arrives for assessment after quietly changing his lunches for three weeks.
hook: Jonas arrives for assessment after quietly changing his lunches for three weeks. His colleagues think he has become a soup enthusiast; he actually misses bread. He says food sticks, then immediately says swallowing hurts, as if those sentences mean exactly the same thing. A half-written restaurant booking sits on his phone because Friday is his anniversary. Before offering any label, you need to learn what happens when he tries to eat, what has changed, and what he can currently swallow.
question: Jonas says food sticks and swallowing hurts. What should you clarify next?
options: Clarify what sticks, what hurts and what is possible now
Write painful swallowing only
Suggest another week of soup first
feedback: The first task is to understand the changed swallowing pattern and its current severity. Recording pain alone loses the sticking sensation and progression. Suggesting more soup before assessment turns an adaptation into a solution and risks leaving a concerning symptom unexplored. Ask rather than assume that fluids are tolerated.
handover: Herr Feld berichtet über seit drei Wochen zunehmende Schluckbeschwerden, zunächst bei Brot, inzwischen mit Schmerzen. Ob Flüssigkeiten und Speichel aktuell problemlos geschluckt werden können, muss noch geklärt werden; die Ursache ist offen.
focus: Separate difficulty from pain

title: The question behind the family photograph
setting: Miriam places a photograph beside her referral letter.
hook: Miriam places a photograph beside her referral letter. Her older brother had cancer, and she has spent the evening matching her swallowing symptoms to his old messages. She is not asking for a lecture about probabilities; she wants to know whether the same story is beginning again. Her husband has helpfully printed eighteen internet pages, including two advertisements for printer ink. She reports new trouble with meals. No examination or investigation has yet established the cause of her symptoms.
question: Miriam asks you to promise her swallowing symptoms are not cancer. How should you respond?
options: Say that family history makes cancer certain
Acknowledge the fear and explain what remains unknown
Say she is worrying unnecessarily
feedback: Acknowledgment allows Miriam to hear the next step rather than defend her fear. Family experience matters to her, but it does not establish her diagnosis. Dismissing the concern may end useful disclosure. Give an honest uncertainty statement and a concrete plan for obtaining and discussing further information.
handover: Frau Vogt berichtet über neu aufgetretene Schluckbeschwerden und ausgeprägte Krebsangst nach der Erkrankung ihres Bruders. Eine Diagnose ist bisher nicht gesichert; die genaue Familienanamnese und weitere Abklärung stehen aus.
focus: Acknowledge cancer fear without predicting diagnosis

title: The answer lost beside the noisy trolley
setting: Armin answers yes to nearly every question about his swallowing.
hook: Armin answers yes to nearly every question about his swallowing. At first the interview seems unusually efficient. Then a trolley rattles past and he asks whether you wanted his postcode or his tablets. His hearing aid is in place, but the room is noisy and you have been speaking while facing the computer. He has brought a careful food diary with larger handwriting than the hospital form allows. A clear account requires a change in the conversation environment, not louder medical vocabulary.
question: Armin may not have heard the earlier questions. What should happen to those answers?
options: Treat every earlier yes as confirmed
Ask his companion everything instead
Improve hearing conditions and revisit uncertain answers
feedback: Changing the environment makes a reliable conversation possible. Earlier answers may need checking because the questions were not heard. Moving immediately to a companion removes Armin from his own consultation. Invite support if he wants it, while continuing to address him and checking the account with him.
handover: Herr Seidel berichtet über Schluckbeschwerden und Schwierigkeiten, Fragen bei Hintergrundlärm zu verstehen. Frühere Ja-Antworten sind noch nicht verlässlich bestätigt; die Anamnese wird unter verbesserten Hörbedingungen erneut erhoben.
focus: Adapt communication for hearing access

title: A camera, not a promise
setting: Elena has been told that an upper endoscopy may help investigate her swallowing problem.
hook: Elena has been told that an upper endoscopy may help investigate her swallowing problem. She imagines a camera the size of the one her nephew takes birdwatching and has already decided it will not fit. She jokes about this, then asks whether agreeing to the discussion means agreeing to the procedure. The clinician responsible for consent has not yet reviewed her individual circumstances. Your task is to make the purpose understandable and create room for questions, rather than obtain a quick signature.
question: Elena thinks listening to an endoscopy explanation means she has consented. What should you do?
options: Explain purpose and invite questions before any consent decision
Promise the procedure cannot hurt or cause complications
Ask for the signature before discussing concerns
feedback: The useful move creates informed participation. A blanket promise about comfort or complications would be misleading. A signature collected before questions are addressed does not demonstrate understanding. Keep the language clear, make space for refusal or further discussion, and leave individual procedural advice to the responsible team.
handover: Frau Brandt hat Fragen zur vorgeschlagenen ÖGD bei Schluckbeschwerden, insbesondere zu Ablauf und Einwilligung. Eine individuelle Aufklärung einschließlich Risiken und Alternativen sowie ihre Entscheidung stehen noch aus.
focus: Explain proposed endoscopy and invite consent questions

title: The tablet with three possible names
setting: Farid opens a phone photograph of his medication box before a discussion about investigations.
hook: Farid opens a phone photograph of his medication box before a discussion about investigations. The picture is mostly a thumb. He remembers that one medicine affects clotting but cannot recall its name or why it was prescribed. His swallowing problem has made taking tablets harder, and he asks whether he should simply leave that one out tonight. The family group chat supplies three confident answers in three minutes. You have no verified medication list and no individual instruction from the procedure team.
question: Farid asks whether to omit an unidentified blood-thinning medicine tonight. What is the next step?
options: Tell him to stop every clotting medicine tonight
Verify the medicine and obtain an individual plan
Choose the first name suggested by the family chat
feedback: Verification is necessary before discussing a medicine change. The photo and group chat do not establish the prescription. A universal stopping instruction ignores why the medicine is used and the planned procedure. Document the uncertainty and give Farid a named route to receive the responsible clinician’s advice.
handover: Herr Neumann berichtet über eine gerinnungshemmende Medikation, deren Präparat und Indikation derzeit unbekannt sind, sowie erschwerte Tabletteneinnahme. Vor einer Änderung ist eine individuelle Rücksprache nach Verifikation des Medikamentenplans erforderlich.
focus: Reconcile medicines without guessing or stopping treatment

title: When saliva will not go down
setting: Klara is halfway through describing weeks of swallowing difficulty when she says she can no longer swallow her saliva.
hook: Klara is halfway through describing weeks of swallowing difficulty when she says she can no longer swallow her saliva. She is distressed and repeatedly spits into a tissue. The routine form still has empty sections about occupation and previous operations. A colleague offers to finish typing while you continue asking questions. This is no longer an exercise in completing a tidy history. You need to communicate the change, stop the routine interview and summon the clinical team for urgent assessment without waiting for the remaining background information.
question: Klara can no longer swallow her saliva. What takes priority over the unfinished history?
options: Finish the operations section before calling anyone
Offer a drink to test whether she really cannot swallow
Stop the routine interview and summon urgent clinical assessment
feedback: Urgent clinical assessment takes priority over completion of routine questions. Asking for another swallowing attempt is not a harmless interview technique here. The handover should identify the current inability to handle saliva and distress, not assume cancer or a specific obstruction before the team evaluates the situation.
handover: Frau Winter gibt an, aktuell keinen Speichel mehr schlucken zu können; sie wirkt deutlich belastet und spuckt wiederholt aus. Das Routinegespräch wird unterbrochen und das Behandlungsteam sofort zur dringlichen Beurteilung hinzugezogen; die Ursache ist unklar.
focus: Recognise inability to swallow saliva as urgent deterioration

title: The lunch conversation that belongs to her
setting: Ruth’s daughter arrives with a colour-coded folder and answers the first four questions about her mother’s swallowing.
hook: Ruth’s daughter arrives with a colour-coded folder and answers the first four questions about her mother’s swallowing. Ruth looks at the floor whenever the discussion turns to weight or alcohol. The daughter has done a great deal of practical work and is clearly worried, but Ruth has not been asked whether she wants the whole consultation shared. Her own notebook says “ask alone” on the back cover. You notice it when she turns a page, without assuming what the private subject might be.
question: Ruth wants private time but also wants her daughter involved later. How should you organise the discussion?
options: Offer private time and agree what may later be shared
Give all details to the daughter because she brought the folder
Demand that Ruth explain her private concern in front of her daughter
feedback: Asking Ruth directly respects her control over the discussion and may uncover information she has not felt able to disclose. The daughter’s involvement does not automatically authorise every disclosure. Requiring a public explanation defeats the point of private time. Thank the helper while preserving the patient’s voice and choices.
handover: Frau Kessler wünscht einen vertraulichen Gesprächsabschnitt zur Anamnese ihrer Schluckbeschwerden. Die Tochter soll nach ihrem Wunsch später zur Besprechung der nächsten Schritte hinzukommen; der Umfang der erlaubten Weitergabe ist noch abzustimmen.
focus: Negotiate a relative’s presence

title: The belt is not a laboratory result
setting: Nils says he has lost “about a stone, perhaps three kilos” since swallowing became uncomfortable.
hook: Nils says he has lost “about a stone, perhaps three kilos” since swallowing became uncomfortable. His belt is two holes tighter, but the household scales have been used mainly to weigh parcels for his online bookshop. He also mentions that he stopped buying lunch because meals take too long. The referral says weight loss without a figure. You need a useful account for colleagues without converting a vivid everyday description into a precise measurement that nobody actually made.
question: Nils reports a looser belt without any weight measurements. How should you record the change?
options: Convert two belt holes into an exact kilogram loss
Document unmeasured change and clarify intake and timeframe
Ignore the concern because no scale reading exists
feedback: The observation deserves attention even without a number. Inventing a conversion creates false precision, while dismissing it loses a potentially important change. Record the patient’s description, the period involved and the missing measurement. Ask what has made meals difficult instead of assuming that appetite alone explains the change.
handover: Herr Hartmann berichtet über seit etwa einem Monat lockereren Gürtel und reduzierte Nahrungsaufnahme bei Schluckbeschwerden. Eine Gewichtsabnahme ist nicht gemessen; Ausmaß und genaue Ursache der verminderten Aufnahme sind noch zu klären.
focus: Separate measured weight change from impression

title: Not the coffee she ordered
setting: Eva is being assessed for upper abdominal discomfort when she mentions that her vomit looked like coffee grounds this morning.
hook: Eva is being assessed for upper abdominal discomfort when she mentions that her vomit looked like coffee grounds this morning. She has also felt faint. Until now, everyone has been discussing whether the cafeteria coffee was too strong. The ordinary conversation stops at this new information. You have no observations, examination findings or confirmed cause yet. The immediate task is to communicate possible bleeding and obtain urgent clinical help, rather than finish a detailed food diary or accept the drink explanation.
question: Eva reports coffee-ground vomit and faintness. What should happen now?
options: Escalate possible bleeding immediately
Complete the meal questionnaire first
Reassure her that coffee explains the colour
feedback: The reported appearance and faintness require urgent assessment, not a conversational explanation based on her last drink. Completing a routine questionnaire delays that response. The right handover communicates the concern and missing observations without pretending that an ulcer or the extent of blood loss has already been established.
handover: Frau Renner berichtet über kaffeesatzartiges Erbrechen und Schwindel. Bei Verdacht auf eine gastrointestinale Blutung wird das Routinegespräch unterbrochen und das Behandlungsteam sofort hinzugezogen; Vitalparameter und Blutungsquelle sind bisher nicht bekannt.
focus: Escalate reported gastrointestinal bleeding

title: The pharmacy in the coat pocket
setting: Tobias says he takes no medication, then empties a coat pocket onto the desk: headache tablets, back-pain tablets and a blister from his neighbour.
hook: Tobias says he takes no medication, then empties a coat pocket onto the desk: headache tablets, back-pain tablets and a blister from his neighbour. He considers these ordinary shopping, not medicines. His upper abdominal burning has been bothering him for weeks, and the tablets let him finish a kitchen renovation that has outlived two promised completion dates. None of the packages proves how often he takes them. You need a nonjudgmental account of actual use rather than a lecture about the untidy pocket.
question: Tobias excludes shop-bought tablets from his medication history. How should you clarify it?
options: Record no medication from his first answer
Review all products and actual use without blame
Assume every package is taken exactly as printed
feedback: The next step is reconciliation, not accusation. The first answer reflected Tobias’s definition of medication and is incomplete. Labels cannot show actual use or borrowed products. Clarify what he takes, how often and why, so the clinician can assess relevance to his symptoms with a reliable list.
handover: Herr Berg berichtet über seit Wochen bestehendes Oberbauchbrennen und zunächst nicht als Medikation eingeordnete Schmerzmittel. Präparate und tatsächliche Einnahme werden anhand der mitgebrachten Packungen geklärt; ein kausaler Zusammenhang ist noch nicht gesichert.
focus: Ask about nonprescription pain medicines

title: Stress has an excellent publicist
setting: Lena works between two offices and thinks her stomach pain must be stress because both office calendars say everything is urgent.
hook: Lena works between two offices and thinks her stomach pain must be stress because both office calendars say everything is urgent. She laughs that even the printer has deadlines. She reports recurring upper abdominal pain, but nobody has yet clarified its timing, accompanying symptoms or medication history. Her explanation may matter, yet it is not a completed assessment. You want to acknowledge a demanding life without allowing the most convenient story to prevent careful questioning about the symptoms themselves.
question: Lena thinks stress explains her recurring abdominal pain. What is the best next move?
options: Confirm stress as the cause immediately
Ignore her work situation completely
Explore symptoms while acknowledging workload
feedback: The useful response holds both parts of the story: significant pressure and an unexplained symptom. Certainty about stress would be premature; ignoring it would miss Lena’s experience and priorities. Ask the necessary clinical questions, avoid invented negative findings, and make the next assessment step understandable rather than dismissive.
handover: Frau Paul berichtet über wiederkehrende Oberbauchschmerzen bei hoher beruflicher Belastung. Ein ursächlicher Zusammenhang mit Stress ist nicht gesichert; zeitlicher Verlauf, Begleitsymptome und Medikation müssen noch erhoben werden.
focus: Avoid attributing symptoms to stress prematurely
topicTitle: The stomach has entered the chat

title: The calendar on the dinner plate
setting: Martin initially says his pain comes after meals.
hook: Martin initially says his pain comes after meals. Later he mentions being awake with it before breakfast and having pain while waiting for today’s appointment. He is not contradicting himself: the pattern has changed. He brings a shopping receipt because it is the only dated paper he could find, and circles the day things became worse. Your handover needs to preserve that change instead of forcing the whole story into the first phrase that fitted neatly into the form.
question: Martin’s pain has changed from after meals to other times too. How should the history reflect that?
options: Document the earlier pattern and the new change
Keep only the first after-meal description
Tell him his answers are inconsistent
feedback: A two-phase account preserves meaningful progression. Retaining only the first answer would make the current problem sound unchanged. Accusing Martin of inconsistency may discourage correction. Clarify timing and present severity, assess whether urgent review is needed, and explicitly distinguish what he reports from findings not yet obtained.
handover: Herr Ehlers berichtet zunächst über postprandiale Oberbauchschmerzen, seit Montag jedoch auch über Schmerzen unabhängig von Mahlzeiten. Die aktuelle Stärke und weitere Begleitsymptome sind noch zu klären; die Veränderung wird zur ärztlichen Neubewertung weitergegeben.
focus: Clarify a changing pain pattern
topicTitle: The stomach has entered the chat

title: A breath test is not a personality test
setting: Sofia hears the name Helicobacter and writes “helicopter” in her notebook.
hook: Sofia hears the name Helicobacter and writes “helicopter” in her notebook. She catches the mistake herself and smiles, but the long word has distracted her from what the proposed test is meant to establish. She has persistent upper abdominal symptoms and asks whether a breath test will show every possible cause. No result is available. Your task is to explain the specific question a test addresses, then separate that question from the wider assessment and any individual preparation instructions.
question: Sofia expects a Helicobacter test to answer every stomach question. What should you explain?
options: Promise a negative result excludes all stomach disease
Explain the test’s question and its limits
Give generic medicine-stopping instructions without checking the test
feedback: Clear limits protect against false reassurance and confusion after the result. A negative result is not a universal answer to persistent symptoms. Unchecked preparation advice can also be inappropriate. Keep the explanation specific, verify understanding and ensure Sofia receives the correct instructions from the team arranging her test.
handover: Frau Kramer fragt bei persistierenden Oberbauchbeschwerden nach der Aussagekraft eines geplanten Helicobacter-Tests. Ein Ergebnis liegt nicht vor; Testart, individuelle Vorbereitung und weitere Befundbesprechung müssen bestätigt werden.
focus: Explain test purpose without claiming a result
topicTitle: The stomach has entered the chat

title: The red sticker needs a story
setting: Dennis’s chart has a red allergy sticker but no substance or reaction.
hook: Dennis’s chart has a red allergy sticker but no substance or reaction. He remembers a rash after a plaster and swollen lips after a medicine many years ago, but is unsure which medicine. He calls both “my usual allergy” and would rather move on to his stomach pain. A sticker can attract attention without supplying useful information. You need to recover the two separate histories, preserve what is uncertain and ensure the team sees the potentially important reaction before making medication or procedure plans.
question: Dennis recalls two different reactions but one drug name is missing. How should you document this?
options: Record allergy to every medicine
Delete the alert because he cannot remember the name
Separate reactions and flag the unknown medicine
feedback: The right move preserves meaningful information and its limits. Labelling all medicines creates inaccurate restrictions, while deleting the history discards a potentially significant reaction. Document what Dennis recalls, identify the unresolved substance and seek records. His current discomfort matters, but the incomplete alert should not be silently accepted as complete.
handover: Herr Roth berichtet über Ausschlag nach Pflasterkontakt und eine frühere Lippenschwellung nach einem namentlich unbekannten Medikament. Die Reaktionen werden getrennt dokumentiert und dem Behandlungsteam mitgeteilt; frühere Unterlagen stehen noch aus.
focus: Distinguish adverse reactions accurately

title: The result that vanished into Tuesday
setting: Anja had an investigation for stomach symptoms and was told someone would call.
hook: Anja had an investigation for stomach symptoms and was told someone would call. It is now Tuesday, although nobody specified which Tuesday. She has checked her phone more often than her kettle and is unsure whether silence means everything was normal. You can see that a result is pending, but you cannot give a release time. This conversation is about replacing a vague promise with a traceable follow-up plan while checking whether her symptoms have changed since the original assessment.
question: Anja assumes no callback means a normal result. What should replace that assumption?
options: Confirm result ownership and a follow-up contact route
Interpret no call as a normal result
Promise the laboratory will finish this afternoon
feedback: A named responsibility and route for questions make the next step usable. Neither silence nor an optimistic deadline establishes a result. Check the current symptom situation as well; a waiting plan should not prevent reassessment if the problem changes. Document the arrangement so colleagues do not repeat the same vague promise.
handover: Frau Winter wartet nach Abklärung von Magenbeschwerden auf einen noch ausstehenden Befund. Zuständigkeit und Rückmeldeweg werden geklärt; der aktuelle Beschwerdeverlauf ist erneut zu erfragen, ein unauffälliges Ergebnis darf nicht angenommen werden.
focus: Close the loop on pending results

title: Yes is not always understanding
setting: Omar nods through an explanation of planned assessment for upper abdominal pain.
hook: Omar nods through an explanation of planned assessment for upper abdominal pain. When the appointment ends, he asks reception whether he should arrive at the laboratory or the endoscopy unit. The written note contains several abbreviations and an arrow that could reasonably point anywhere. He is embarrassed because he works as a teacher and thinks he should understand forms. The communication repair is yours to make: simplify the next step and check whether your explanation was usable without turning him into a pupil being marked.
question: Omar nodded but cannot identify where to go next. How should you repair the explanation?
options: Ask whether he understood everything again
Verify the plan and ask him to explain the first step back
Repeat the same abbreviations more loudly
feedback: A concrete description of the first action reveals whether the explanation works. Another broad yes-or-no question may produce the same polite nod. Louder jargon remains jargon. Confirm the real plan before simplifying it, so improved wording does not accidentally make an unverified sequence sound official or complete.
handover: Herr Lind hat den organisatorischen Ablauf der geplanten Abklärung seiner Oberbauchbeschwerden nicht verstanden. Der bestätigte nächste Schritt wird erneut erklärt und rückgefragt; eine durch Nicken belegte Verständnissicherung liegt nicht vor.
focus: Use teach-back without testing the patient
topicTitle: The stomach has entered the chat

title: The croissant is not on trial
setting: Benno points to breakfast as if the croissant has hired a lawyer.
hook: Benno points to breakfast as if the croissant has hired a lawyer. He has had episodes of upper abdominal pain and thinks admitting what he eats will earn a lecture. He says “nothing unusual” until you explain that timing matters more than judging the menu. Today he is attending a review after an earlier assessment; no current examination findings are supplied. Your challenge is to explore where the pain starts, how long it lasts and whether it changes, without making one food into a diagnosis.
question: Benno is worried you will blame his breakfast. How can you obtain a useful pain history?
options: Ask neutrally about timing, location and duration
Blame the croissant and end the history
Diagnose gallstones from the meal alone
feedback: The correct move obtains useful symptom information without judgment. Blame can suppress details, while diagnosing from a meal gives one clue more certainty than it deserves. Clarify the present situation and previous assessment, and retain uncertainty about the cause until the responsible clinician evaluates the available evidence.
handover: Herr Falk berichtet über Oberbauchschmerzepisoden in zeitlichem Zusammenhang mit Mahlzeiten. Lokalisation, Dauer und aktueller Verlauf werden konkretisiert; eine biliäre Ursache ist anhand der bisherigen Angaben nicht gesichert.
focus: Explore food timing without moral judgment

title: The gel is the least mysterious part
setting: Tessa is waiting for an abdominal ultrasound after an assessment of pain.
hook: Tessa is waiting for an abdominal ultrasound after an assessment of pain. She knows ultrasound from a relative’s pregnancy and wonders why it has appeared in her appointment list. She is more worried about what the screen might show than the cold gel, though she jokes that the gel never receives a weather forecast. You are explaining the examination, not interpreting a result that does not exist. A simple account should cover what happens and why the team has proposed it, without guaranteeing that it answers everything.
question: Tessa expects ultrasound to identify every cause of pain. What explanation would help?
options: Promise the scan will identify every possible cause
Explain what the scan does and what it cannot promise
Dismiss the question because ultrasound is routine
feedback: The useful explanation gives Tessa a picture of the process and realistic expectations. Calling it routine does not answer her concern. Promising every cause will be found is inaccurate. Ask what she would like clarified, then let the subsequent findings, rather than a reassuring guess, guide the result discussion.
handover: Frau König hat Fragen zur geplanten Abdomensonografie bei Oberbauchbeschwerden. Ein Untersuchungsbefund liegt noch nicht vor; Zweck und Ablauf werden erklärt, ohne eine vollständige Ursachenklärung zu garantieren.
focus: Explain ultrasound in ordinary language

title: A new colour changes the conversation
setting: Hanna was discussing intermittent abdominal pain when she adds that her eyes have looked yellow since yesterday and she is now shivering.
hook: Hanna was discussing intermittent abdominal pain when she adds that her eyes have looked yellow since yesterday and she is now shivering. She has not had a current clinical assessment. Her husband wants to read out the previous ultrasound report first, but the new symptoms matter more than completing that document review. This scene contains no comic detour. Your task is to identify the change clearly, stop routine questioning and summon the clinical team promptly rather than assume that a known gallstone explains everything safely.
question: Hanna now reports yellow eyes and shivering with abdominal pain. What should happen first?
options: Read the entire previous report before escalating
Say jaundice is normal with any gallstone
Summon the clinical team for the new symptoms now
feedback: The changed symptoms require prompt assessment. Reading the whole report first delays that response, while calling jaundice normal risks false reassurance. State what Hanna reports and what remains unmeasured. The old information may help the assessment, but it should accompany urgent action rather than become a condition for starting it.
handover: Frau Lorenz berichtet bei Bauchschmerzen über seit gestern gelbliche Augen und aktuellen Schüttelfrost. Das Behandlungsteam wird sofort zur dringlichen Beurteilung hinzugezogen; Vitalparameter, Untersuchungsbefund und Ursache sind noch unbekannt.
focus: Escalate pain with reported jaundice and shivering

title: The operation and the school play
setting: Mara asks whether she can have surgery on Thursday and attend her daughter’s school play on Friday.
hook: Mara asks whether she can have surgery on Thursday and attend her daughter’s school play on Friday. The family has arranged the scenery, costumes and a backup parent; nobody has arranged a backup abdomen. She has been referred to discuss symptomatic gallstones but has not yet had a surgical assessment. Her question is really about being present for her child and organising help. You need to take that seriously without promising a procedure, a date or a recovery that has not been individually discussed.
question: Mara needs to plan around a school play after possible surgery. What can you responsibly offer?
options: Explore her priorities and obtain individual planning advice
Guarantee attendance the day after surgery
Tell her family plans are irrelevant
feedback: The right response respects the family commitment while keeping the medical plan honest. A guaranteed next-day activity is unsupported before individual assessment. Dismissing the school event misses why Mara is asking. Prepare specific questions for the responsible team and distinguish confirmed arrangements from possibilities still under discussion.
handover: Frau Albers möchte eine mögliche Operation und familiäre Verpflichtungen abstimmen. Indikation, Termin und individuelle Belastbarkeit nach dem Eingriff sind noch nicht festgelegt; diese Fragen werden für das chirurgische Gespräch gesammelt.
focus: Discuss planning uncertainty and practical priorities

title: Two procedures, two different questions
setting: Rainer’s notes contain two unfamiliar words: ERCP and cholecystectomy.
hook: Rainer’s notes contain two unfamiliar words: ERCP and cholecystectomy. He assumes they are competing spellings for the same operation. His friend has drawn a plumbing diagram on an envelope, but the liver appears to be connected to the kitchen sink. You have been asked to help him understand the distinction before a specialist discussion. No individual procedure has been confirmed in this scene. Explain the anatomy simply and the different aims without claiming that one procedure automatically replaces the other.
question: Rainer thinks ERCP and gallbladder surgery are the same procedure. What should you clarify?
options: Say both names mean the same operation
Explain the two structures and check the proposed plan
Promise ERCP will remove every gallbladder stone
feedback: The correct distinction helps Rainer ask informed questions. Treating the terms as synonyms hides their different aims. Promising clearance of gallbladder stones by ERCP misdescribes the procedure. Keep the anatomy simple and connect it to a verified individual plan rather than choosing a treatment from the diagram.
handover: Herr Voss verwechselt ERCP und Cholezystektomie. Der Unterschied zwischen Gallengang und Gallenblase wird erklärt; welche Maßnahme individuell vorgesehen ist, muss anhand der fachärztlichen Planung bestätigt werden.
focus: Distinguish gallbladder from bile duct

title: The stone found while looking elsewhere
setting: Ute’s scan report mentions a gallstone found during an unrelated investigation.
hook: Ute’s scan report mentions a gallstone found during an unrelated investigation. She has booked an appointment because the word stone sounds like an object that must immediately be removed. Her neighbour has offered a dramatic account involving a suitcase and an ambulance, neither of which appears in Ute’s report. Her symptom history has not yet been taken. You need to explain that a finding and the reason for treatment are separate questions, while still exploring whether she has relevant symptoms.
question: Ute has an incidental gallstone report but no symptom history yet. What should you do next?
options: Arrange surgery solely because the report says stone
Guarantee the finding can never cause problems
Clarify the finding and ask about symptoms
feedback: The useful response neither overreacts nor dismisses. A scan finding alone does not establish that surgery is needed, and a permanent guarantee is also unsupported. Ask about symptoms, check the report and make the follow-up plan explicit. Do not document Ute as symptom-free before asking her directly.
handover: Bei Frau Sommer wurde laut Bericht ein Gallenstein im Rahmen einer anderen Untersuchung gefunden. Eine gezielte Beschwerdeanamnese und die Einordnung des Befundes stehen noch aus; Beschwerdefreiheit wird nicht vorausgesetzt.
focus: Explain an incidental finding without overclaiming causation

title: Eight is not a negotiation
setting: Pavel rates his upper abdominal pain as eight and then asks whether that sounds too dramatic.
hook: Pavel rates his upper abdominal pain as eight and then asks whether that sounds too dramatic. He normally repairs industrial ovens and prides himself on staying calm when equipment fails. A colleague has joked that anyone who can carry a toolbox can wait. The assessment has only just begun, and his current condition needs clinical attention. You need to acknowledge his report and obtain useful details without turning the scale into a contest or using his occupation as evidence that the pain is minor.
question: Pavel questions whether his pain score of eight is exaggerated. How should you respond?
options: Acknowledge severity and obtain prompt assessment
Lower the score because he can speak calmly
Ask him to prove pain by repeating a movement
feedback: The correct move takes the reported severity seriously and communicates it for assessment. Calm speech does not justify changing his score. Asking him to demonstrate pain is not needed to believe the report. Keep follow-up questions purposeful, avoid delay and distinguish his description from examination findings not yet available.
handover: Herr Stein gibt aktuelle Oberbauchschmerzen mit einer Intensität von acht von zehn an. Eine zeitnahe klinische Beurteilung wird veranlasst; Lokalisation, Beginn und Begleitsymptome werden situationsgerecht ergänzt, objektive Befunde liegen noch nicht vor.
focus: Validate pain while obtaining useful description

title: The operation that has not happened
setting: Ines hears a trainee say that she has had her gallbladder removed.
hook: Ines hears a trainee say that she has had her gallbladder removed. She is sitting in a clinic to discuss whether that might happen and raises an eyebrow: “I would have liked to attend.” The referral contains the phrase for consideration of surgery, which has become postoperative in the draft summary. No harm has yet been established, but the error could mislead the next team. Your task is to accept the correction, verify the source and repair the record without making Ines responsible for everyone’s documentation.
question: Ines corrects a draft claiming an operation that has not happened. What should you do with the record?
options: Keep the draft because it came from a referral
Verify and correct the planned-versus-completed statement
Tell her the distinction is only administrative
feedback: Verification and correction prevent an unperformed operation from becoming accepted history. A referral can be misread, so its existence does not validate the draft. The distinction matters to subsequent clinical reasoning. Explain the correction, document it appropriately and check any handover that may already have repeated the error.
handover: Frau Wolff stellt klar, dass bisher keine Cholezystektomie erfolgt ist. Die fehlerhafte Übertragung einer geplanten chirurgischen Besprechung als abgeschlossene Operation wird anhand der Vorlage überprüft und in der Dokumentation korrigiert.
focus: Correct planned versus completed care in handover

title: The city map with a different legend
setting: Nora knows every public toilet between home and work.
hook: Nora knows every public toilet between home and work. Her map has stars, opening hours and one establishment marked “key hidden behind enormous plant.” She has had recurrent diarrhoea and abdominal cramps, but says things are manageable because she still gets to the office. The cost is leaving an hour early and avoiding lunch with colleagues. No diagnosis is confirmed. You want to understand the burden of symptoms without making her explain intimate details where other people in the waiting area can hear.
question: Nora still reaches work, but only by planning around toilets. How should you explore the burden?
options: Explore the daily adaptations in private
Call the symptoms mild because she still works
Ask for bowel details loudly at reception
feedback: The useful move uncovers both symptoms and their impact while protecting privacy. Attendance at work does not establish severity or cause. Discussing intimate details within public hearing can stop disclosure. Ask specifically and respectfully, then carry the burden and the remaining diagnostic uncertainty into the clinical summary.
handover: Frau Rehm berichtet über wiederkehrende Diarrhöen und Bauchkrämpfe mit erheblicher Planung des Arbeitswegs nach Toilettenverfügbarkeit. Häufigkeit, nächtliche Beschwerden und weitere Begleitsymptome sind noch zu erheben; eine Diagnose ist nicht gesichert.
focus: Ask about functional impact without embarrassment
topicTitle: Let's talk about the awkward bit

title: The holiday has no alibi
setting: Elias developed diarrhoea during a holiday and his partner stayed well.
hook: Elias developed diarrhoea during a holiday and his partner stayed well. He thinks this proves it cannot be an infection, because they shared a table and argued over the same last potato. The symptoms have continued after returning home. He is worried about inflammatory bowel disease after reading the referral, but no stool results or diagnosis are available. You need to collect exposure and symptom details without accepting either his reassuring shortcut or the opposite shortcut that every holiday symptom must be infectious.
question: Elias thinks an unaffected partner excludes infection. How should you address that conclusion?
options: Exclude infection because his partner is well
Explain the uncertainty and gather the relevant history
Confirm infection solely because symptoms began on holiday
feedback: The correct response avoids both shortcuts. An unaffected partner does not exclude infection, and holiday timing does not prove it. Clarify the course and relevant exposures, including features that may change urgency. Document the possibilities as possibilities while the responsible clinician determines the appropriate assessment.
handover: Herr Werner berichtet über seit einer Reise anhaltende Diarrhöen; die Partnerin sei beschwerdefrei. Daraus lässt sich eine infektiöse Ursache nicht ausschließen; Verlauf, Expositionen und weitere Abklärung sind noch offen.
focus: Avoid excluding infection from an unaffected companion
topicTitle: Let's talk about the awkward bit

title: Three weeks is a duration, not a verdict
setting: Mina says her diarrhoea started eighteen days ago.
hook: Mina says her diarrhoea started eighteen days ago. A draft note calls it chronic and, one line later, says symptoms have lasted less than three weeks. She is worried that chronic means permanent. She has already reorganised her kitchen cupboards for a lifelong diet no clinician has recommended. The immediate teaching opportunity is precise language: document the duration she reports, explain that labels have specific uses and avoid using a time category to decide the cause or predict her future.
question: Mina reads chronic as permanent despite an eighteen-day history. How should you repair the wording?
options: Tell her chronic always means lifelong
Ignore the contradictory dates in the note
Record the exact duration and explain the uncertainty
feedback: Precise duration is the strongest information currently available. Equating an imprecise label with a lifelong condition frightens without evidence. Ignoring the conflict leaves colleagues and patient with different stories. Correct the wording, assess the current problem and explain that the cause still requires evaluation.
handover: Frau Adler gibt eine Diarrhö seit achtzehn Tagen an. Die widersprüchliche Bezeichnung im Entwurf wird präzisiert; aus der Dauer allein lassen sich Ursache und weiterer Verlauf nicht ableiten.
focus: Use exact duration instead of contradictory labels
topicTitle: Let's talk about the awkward bit

title: The red number on the portal
setting: Kai’s online portal has coloured a stool test result red.
hook: Kai’s online portal has coloured a stool test result red. He has photographed the screen, enlarged it and sent it to himself three times, as though a fourth copy might include an explanation. The result is a raised calprotectin value, but the clinician has not reviewed it with him. He asks whether it proves Crohn’s disease. The case is about explaining what a marker can suggest without treating a coloured number as a complete diagnosis or dismissing his concern about the result.
question: Kai thinks a red calprotectin result confirms Crohn’s disease. What should you explain?
options: Explain the marker’s limits and arrange interpretation
Confirm Crohn’s disease from the red result
Tell him portal results never matter
feedback: The useful response connects the result to a clinical review. A raised marker can occur in more than one context, so it cannot establish the diagnosis by itself.
